fallacies.name: A priori argument
fallacies.summary: Treating a conclusion as settled before weighing the evidence, then dismissing contrary results to protect it.
fallacies.body: A priori reasoning starts from premises or principles rather than observation; that method alone is not a fallacy. The defect here is dogmatic rationalization: evidence is allowed to support the conclusion but never to count against it. A failed trial is rejected only because it conflicts with the belief, with no independent reason to doubt the trial.

examples.text: The trial failed, but this treatment always works, so that trial must have been flawed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion is protected from disconfirmation by ad hoc dismissal of contrary evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Reasoning from definitions or mathematical premises without experiment is not this fallacy.
Rejecting evidence for a specific, independently supported methodological flaw is not dogmatic immunization.

fallacies.name: Abusive ad hominem
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a claim by insulting or attacking its speaker instead of answering the claim or evidence.
fallacies.body:
A speaker's character does not by itself determine whether a proposition is true. The inference fails when the personal attack is offered as the reason to reject the proposition, leaving its support untouched.

A design reviewer points out a bridge's load-test failure; a reply says the reviewer is dishonest, therefore the bridge is safe. Evidence that the reviewer has a relevant conflict or poor record may affect how much weight to give their testimony, but it does not establish the bridge's safety; the test still needs an answer.

examples.text: Lena says the bridge failed its load test, but she is a liar, so the bridge is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An attack on the proponent is used in place of evaluating the stated claim or its evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Relevant evidence about a witness's reliability or bias can qualify testimony, provided it is not treated as proof that the contrary claim is true.

fallacies.name: Accent fallacy
fallacies.summary: Changing a statement's meaning by stressing or highlighting a word in a way the original context does not support.
fallacies.body:
Emphasis can alter scope, contrast, or implication. The error occurs when someone treats the emphasized reading as what the statement established, even though the emphasis was absent or the surrounding context rules it out.

A speaker quotes “I said the plan was acceptable” and stresses I to imply nobody else approved it. If the original speaker did stress “I” to correct a claim about who approved the plan, reporting that emphasis is a fair clarification; the fallacy requires a misleading shift in meaning.

examples.text: The note said “the medicine may reduce symptoms”; reading may with heavy stress is used to claim it is almost certain to work.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion depends on a change in spoken or typographic emphasis that changes the statement's apparent meaning.
doesNotCountWhen: Accurately identifying emphasis that was present and relevant to the original meaning is not a fallacy.

fallacies.name: Accident
fallacies.summary: Applying a general rule to an exceptional case where the rule's purpose or conditions do not fit.
fallacies.body:
A rule can be sound for ordinary cases yet misapplied when an unusual circumstance defeats its rationale. The mistake is assuming that because the rule generally applies, it must apply without qualification here.

“Keep out of the water” sensibly protects swimmers at a contaminated beach; a rescuer entering briefly to pull out a drowning child is not thereby acting wrongly. The rule may still apply when the exception does not undermine its purpose, such as someone entering for recreation despite the warning.

examples.text: The park bans vehicles on paths, so an ambulance must not use the path to reach an injured visitor.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A broad rule is applied mechanically to a case whose relevant exceptional features make the rule's rationale inapplicable.
doesNotCountWhen: Applying a rule to an ordinary case within its intended scope is not an accident fallacy.

fallacies.name: Ad fidentia
fallacies.summary: Treating confidence or certainty as if it were evidence that a claim is true.
fallacies.body:
Confidence describes a person's state of belief, not the quality of the reasons for that belief. The inference is defective when assurance substitutes for support: repetition of “I know” cannot bridge a missing evidential step.

A manager insists a shipment arrived because she is completely certain, despite the tracking record showing otherwise. Confidence can be a clue about firsthand memory, but it is not conclusive; checking the record or other corroboration is what bears on the shipment's arrival.

examples.text: I am absolutely certain the report is accurate, so there is no need to check its figures.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's certainty is offered as the main warrant for the claim, without independent supporting reasons.
doesNotCountWhen: Confidence accompanied by relevant evidence is not fallacious; the evidence, rather than confidence itself, supports the claim.

fallacies.name: Ad hoc rescue
fallacies.summary: Inventing an unsupported exception after a claim meets contrary evidence, solely to keep the claim intact.
fallacies.body:
A hypothesis may be revised when new evidence warrants a specific revision. An ad hoc rescue instead adds a convenient, unverified condition only after the prediction fails, and supplies no independent way to test that condition.

Someone predicts a device will work in daylight; it fails, so they say an invisible interference must have occurred, with no evidence for interference and no test that could disprove it. Finding a documented power outage would be a legitimate explanation because it is independently checkable and can be assessed against the event.

examples.text: The forecast said rain today. It stayed dry because the weather system secretly changed direction at the last second; that proves the forecast model is still perfect.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An explanation is added only after disconfirmation and lacks independent evidence or testable consequences.
doesNotCountWhen: A revised explanation supported by new evidence and exposed to further testing is not an ad hoc rescue.

fallacies.name: Affirmative conclusion from a negative premise
fallacies.summary: In categorical logic, drawing an affirmative conclusion when a premise says that some members are excluded.
fallacies.body:
In a valid categorical syllogism, a negative premise requires a negative conclusion: the premise establishes separation, not membership in a shared category. Concluding that two groups overlap or share a positive property goes beyond what the exclusion supports.

“No reptiles are mammals; some pets are not mammals” does not show that some pets are reptiles. A pet could be a bird or fish. If an additional premise identifies those pets as reptiles, an affirmative conclusion may follow from that added information, not from the negative premise alone.

examples.text: No poets are engineers. Some musicians are not engineers. Therefore some musicians are poets.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A categorical argument has a negative premise but asserts an affirmative conclusion not supported by another valid route.
doesNotCountWhen: An affirmative conclusion supported by additional premises that establish membership is not this syllogistic error.

fallacies.name: Affirming a disjunct
fallacies.summary: Treating the truth of one option in an inclusive “A or B” as proof that the other option is false.
fallacies.body:
In an inclusive disjunction, at least one option is true and both may be true. From A or B and A, one cannot infer not-B unless the alternatives are explicitly exclusive.

“The server is in the east region or it is available” does not imply that an eastern server cannot be available. In “the key is either in the left drawer or the right drawer, but not both,” the explicit exclusivity does permit eliminating the right drawer once the left one is confirmed.

examples.text: The notice says the event is indoors or open to members; it is indoors, so nonmembers cannot attend.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument assumes an inclusive disjunction is exclusive and rules out another option without a premise doing so.
doesNotCountWhen: Eliminating an alternative from an explicitly exclusive either/or is valid.

fallacies.name: Affirming the consequent
fallacies.summary: Inferring that a condition occurred because its expected result occurred, although other causes could produce that result.
fallacies.body:
The form is: if P then Q; Q; therefore P. The conditional says P is sufficient for Q, not that P is the only route to Q.

If a sprinkler runs, the lawn gets wet; the lawn is wet; therefore the sprinkler ran. Rain could also have wet it. The inference would be supported if independent information ruled out every relevant alternative cause, or if the premise stated that the lawn is wet only when the sprinkler runs.

examples.text: If the alarm is set, its light flashes. The light is flashing, so the alarm must be set.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion asserts the antecedent solely from the consequent of a one-way conditional.
doesNotCountWhen: A biconditional, or evidence excluding other causes of the consequent, can make the inference valid.

fallacies.name: Alleged certainty
fallacies.summary: Presenting a disputed claim as certain without enough evidence to justify that level of confidence.
fallacies.body:
Some claims are well established, but describing a claim as undeniable does not establish it. The defect is a mismatch between certainty and support, often used to close discussion before relevant uncertainty has been examined.

A consultant calls a projected sales figure “guaranteed” despite relying on a small, uncertain sample. A conclusion can properly be stated confidently when strong, convergent evidence supports it; the label is not the problem when the support warrants it.

examples.text: It is certain that this untested policy will cut costs by half; no further evidence is needed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument uses categorical certainty to conceal unresolved evidence or inferential gaps.
doesNotCountWhen: A confident conclusion is not fallacious when the evidence is sufficiently strong for that degree of confidence.

fallacies.name: Alphabet soup
fallacies.summary: Using unexplained abbreviations or technical labels to make a claim seem supported or authoritative.
fallacies.body:
Specialized vocabulary can communicate precisely among people who share its definitions. It becomes a persuasive defect when jargon replaces the explanation needed to show why the conclusion follows, or prevents an audience from checking the reasoning.

A report says “the QX-7 protocol is optimal due to its RCP profile” but defines neither term nor provides results. Technical shorthand is acceptable when terms are defined or familiar to the audience and the underlying evidence remains available.

examples.text: The proposal is superior because it uses the R-9 architecture and achieves a QCM-4 profile.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Unexplained jargon stands in for the evidence or reasoning the audience needs to assess the claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Accurate technical terms, explained when needed and backed by relevant evidence, are not fallacious.

fallacies.name: Alternative advance
fallacies.summary: Offering a supposed alternative that does not actually answer the problem or support the conclusion being advanced.
fallacies.body:
A proposal can look like an alternative while avoiding the choice or issue under discussion. The flaw is in treating an unrelated or inadequate option as if it resolves the stated problem.

Asked how to reduce a queue, a manager says people should arrive earlier, although the bottleneck is a single slow service counter and arrival time does not increase capacity. Earlier arrival might help when demand peaks at a predictable time and the queue is caused by simultaneous arrivals; that causal link must be shown.

examples.text: We need a safer crossing, so people should simply be more careful when crossing the busy road.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The proposed alternative is presented as a solution although it does not address the causal problem or stated requirement.
doesNotCountWhen: A proposal that addresses the problem through a supported mechanism is a genuine alternative even if it is imperfect.

fallacies.name: Alternative truth
fallacies.summary: Claiming a statement is true by appeal to a preferred or convenient version of truth rather than shared evidence or standards.
fallacies.body:
The phrase is used for shifting what counts as truth so a favored claim can survive challenge. Instead of answering evidence under an agreed method, the speaker substitutes a personal, political, or rhetorical criterion and treats that substitution as verification.

A seller says a product “is true for me” after its measured performance claim fails. Personal meaning can be valid evidence about someone's experience; it does not verify a separate factual claim about measured performance.

examples.text: The test shows the device failed, but my truth is that it passed, so the advertised claim is true.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker changes the criterion of truth in response to contrary evidence and presents the preferred criterion as proof of a factual claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Stating that experiences or values differ is not fallacious when it is not offered as evidence for an objective factual conclusion.

fallacies.name: Ambiguity fallacy
fallacies.summary: Using a word or phrase with different meanings across an argument so the conclusion seems to follow.
fallacies.body:
An argument needs its key terms to keep a stable meaning. If a premise uses a term one way and the conclusion relies on another, the apparent connection is verbal rather than logical.

“Feathers are light; what is light cannot be dark; therefore feathers cannot be dark” shifts from low weight to brightness. A word with several senses is harmless when context makes the intended sense clear and the reasoning does not trade on the shift.

examples.text: The bank is beside the river; a bank is a financial institution; therefore a financial institution is beside the river.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A key expression changes sense between premises and conclusion, creating an invalid apparent inference.
doesNotCountWhen: Using a polysemous word consistently in one clear sense is not equivocation.

fallacies.name: Amphiboly
fallacies.summary: Drawing a conclusion from a sentence whose grammatical structure permits more than one reading.
fallacies.body:
Unlike a shift in a single word's meaning, amphiboly arises from syntax or attachment: it is unclear which phrase modifies which person or action. The argument selects the reading that favors its conclusion without establishing that reading.

“Riley saw the doctor with binoculars” could mean Riley used binoculars or the doctor had them. A speaker may resolve the ambiguity by clarifying the intended grammar; the error occurs when an ambiguous wording is treated as unambiguous evidence.

examples.text: The headline says “Local council to discuss dog bite cases”; the report concludes the council will discuss cases involving dogs that bite, although the phrase could describe cases where dogs were bitten.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion depends on one disputed grammatical reading of an ambiguous sentence.
doesNotCountWhen: Clarifying the intended grammatical relation before drawing a conclusion removes the ambiguity.

fallacies.name: Anecdotal fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating a personal story or vivid individual case as enough to establish a broad pattern or causal claim.
fallacies.body:
Anecdotes can show that an event is possible and can suggest questions worth investigating. They usually cannot establish how common an outcome is or whether one factor caused it, because the case may be unusual and lacks a comparison group.

One person felt better after taking a supplement; that does not show the supplement works for most people or caused the change. A carefully documented case can support a narrow claim about what happened to that individual, while broader claims need representative data or controlled comparison.

examples.text: My neighbor used this remedy and recovered, so the remedy cures the illness.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: One or a few selected cases are used as sufficient evidence for a general frequency or causal conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Anecdotes are relevant to illustrate a possibility or generate a hypothesis, provided they are not treated as decisive population evidence.

fallacies.name: Anonymous authority
fallacies.summary: Treating an unnamed or uncheckable source's asserted expertise as proof of a claim.
fallacies.body:
An appeal to expertise can be useful when the expert's identity, relevant qualifications, and basis for the claim can be assessed. “Experts say” hides those checks and makes it impossible to judge whether the source is qualified, accurately represented, or independent.

A post says unnamed doctors have proved a supplement safe but gives no names or study. A confidential source may still merit attention if a reliable reporter explains their relevant access and corroborates the claim; anonymity alone neither proves nor disproves it.

examples.text: Experts agree that the new machine is harmless, but the speaker will not identify them or describe their evidence.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An unnamed or untraceable authority is the central support and the audience cannot assess its relevant expertise or claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Anonymity does not invalidate a claim when the source's relevant basis is explained and independently corroborated.

fallacies.name: Anthropomorphic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Explaining a nonhuman system by assigning it human intentions or feelings without evidence for those mental states.
fallacies.body:
Personification can be a useful metaphor, but it does not establish what a natural process, animal, or machine is doing. The inference fails when an attributed motive is treated as the causal explanation instead of examining mechanisms and evidence.

“The thermostat wants the room to be warm” is shorthand for its control mechanism, not evidence of desire. Saying a system “is trying” to reach a setpoint can be harmless if the speaker makes clear that this describes a designed function rather than a human-like intention.

examples.text: The river flooded because it was angry at the town, so the town should apologize to it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A human motive or emotion is attributed to a nonhuman thing and used as an explanation or evidential premise.
doesNotCountWhen: Figurative language or shorthand for a demonstrable function is not fallacious when it is not treated as literal motive.

fallacies.name: Appeal to accomplishment
fallacies.summary: Treating someone's achievement or effort as proof that their claim is correct.
fallacies.body:
A person's accomplishments can establish relevant experience, but they do not make every statement true. The reasoning fails when status or past success substitutes for evidence about the particular claim at issue.

A celebrated engineer says a bridge is safe, and a committee accepts that without examining the inspection data. The engineer's track record may be relevant testimony; the conclusion still depends on whether the expertise fits the question and the evidence is sound.

examples.text: She has built ten successful companies, so her prediction that this drug is safe must be right.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Achievement is used as the decisive warrant for a claim beyond what that achievement establishes.
doesNotCountWhen: Relevant expertise and a strong record can reasonably affect credibility when paired with evidence suited to the claim.

fallacies.name: Appeal to age
fallacies.summary: Treating a claim as true or false solely because it is old or new.
fallacies.body:
Age alone does not establish correctness. A longstanding practice may persist for good reasons or from habit; a new proposal may be promising or untested. The argument substitutes chronology for evidence about the claim's merits.

A policy is defended because it has existed for generations, without showing it works. Long use can provide useful evidence about consequences when those consequences have been observed and compared; mere longevity is not proof.

examples.text: This rule is centuries old, so it must be the best way to decide cases.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The age or recency of an idea is the main reason offered for accepting or rejecting it.
doesNotCountWhen: Historical track record or current evidence about performance may support a claim; the date alone does not.

fallacies.name: Appeal to anger
fallacies.summary: Using anger to make an audience accept a claim without answering its evidence.
fallacies.body: Anger may be justified and can motivate action, but emotional intensity does not establish the factual premise or proposed remedy. The defect is using outrage as the warrant instead of showing why the conclusion follows.

examples.text: Anyone who questions this report is helping the people who caused the disaster, so the report must be right.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Indignation or hostility is offered in place of support for the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Anger can accompany a well-supported argument; the argument is sound when its reasons carry the conclusion.

fallacies.name: Appeal to celebrity
fallacies.summary: Using a famous person's endorsement as evidence outside the person's relevant expertise.
fallacies.body: Fame gives visibility, not special knowledge of every subject. A celebrity may have relevant training, but the endorsement alone does not demonstrate the claim or the quality of its evidence.

examples.text: A famous actor says this investment is safe, so it is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Public recognition is the principal reason for accepting a claim unrelated to the person's expertise.
doesNotCountWhen: A celebrity with directly relevant expertise may offer testimony, which should still be weighed by its basis and corroboration.

fallacies.name: Appeal to closure
fallacies.summary: Treating the desire to end uncertainty or discussion as evidence that a conclusion is true.
fallacies.body: Closure is a psychological need, not a test of truth. Declaring a matter settled because continued inquiry is uncomfortable can hide unanswered evidence or alternatives.

examples.text: We need to move on, so the first explanation must be correct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument relies on the audience's desire for finality rather than reasons that settle the issue.
doesNotCountWhen: Ending inquiry after adequate evidence and a stated decision rule is not fallacious.

fallacies.name: Appeal to coincidence
fallacies.summary: Dismissing a meaningful pattern as coincidence without assessing how likely it is under competing explanations.
fallacies.body: Coincidence is possible, but naming it does not explain a pattern. Conversely, a striking coincidence alone does not prove a causal or intentional connection; the relevant rates and alternatives matter.

examples.text: Three alarms failed on the same night; it is just coincidence, so no inspection is needed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: “Coincidence” is used as a complete explanation without comparing likelihoods or checking a plausible common cause.
doesNotCountWhen: Calling an event coincidental can be reasonable when base rates and evidence show it is unsurprising.

fallacies.name: Appeal to common belief
fallacies.summary: Treating widespread belief as proof that a claim is true.
fallacies.body: Agreement can reflect shared evidence, but it can also arise from tradition, incentives, or common error. The number of believers does not by itself establish the proposition.

examples.text: Everyone in the office thinks the supplier is reliable, so the supplier's figures need no audit.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Popularity of a belief substitutes for evidence about its truth.
doesNotCountWhen: Consensus among informed, independent experts can be evidence when it results from relevant methods and evidence, not mere headcount.

fallacies.name: Appeal to common folk
fallacies.summary: Treating a claim as true because ordinary people accept it, or false because experts do.
fallacies.body: The social identity of believers does not decide whether their claim is correct. The appeal exploits a contrast between “ordinary people” and an out-group instead of examining reasons.

examples.text: Real people know the new vaccine is dangerous; only elites deny it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A claim is endorsed or rejected by invoking ordinary people as a class rather than evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Public experience can supply relevant observations, but those observations still need evaluation.

fallacies.name: Appeal to common practice
fallacies.summary: Treating a practice as acceptable or correct because many people do it.
fallacies.body: Common behavior may indicate convenience or convention, not safety, legality, or morality. The inference needs a reason connecting prevalence to the judgment being made.

examples.text: Everyone shares passwords at work, so sharing this account password is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Frequency of behavior is offered as sufficient support for its acceptability or truth.
doesNotCountWhen: A widespread practice can be evidence of a norm or useful precedent when that is the actual question.

fallacies.name: Appeal to common sense
fallacies.summary: Using “common sense” as a substitute for explaining why a claim follows.
fallacies.body: Intuitions can be useful starting points, but they vary and can fail in unfamiliar or technical cases. Invoking common sense merely asserts that disagreement is unreasonable; it does not expose the missing reasoning.

examples.text: Common sense says the heavier object falls faster, so there is no need to measure it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The label “obvious” or “common sense” stands in for relevant grounds.
doesNotCountWhen: A clear intuitive judgment may be reasonable when the context is familiar and evidence does not challenge it.

fallacies.name: Appeal to complexity
fallacies.summary: Assuming a claim is true because the subject is too complicated for the audience to check.
fallacies.body: Complexity can limit what a person can verify directly, but it does not make a conclusion correct. The argument uses the difficulty of scrutiny to demand acceptance instead of supplying accessible grounds or accountable expertise.

examples.text: The model proves the policy works; its equations are too complicated to show you.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Complexity is used to block scrutiny and is treated as support for the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Relying provisionally on a qualified expert for a complex topic is reasonable when methods and relevant credentials are open to review.

fallacies.name: Appeal to consequences
fallacies.summary: Judging whether a claim is true by whether its consequences would be welcome or frightening.
fallacies.body: A proposition's desirability does not establish its truth. Consequences are relevant to whether an action should be taken, but factual predictions still need evidence independent of the preference.

examples.text: If the audit found fraud, the company would collapse; therefore there was no fraud.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument accepts or rejects a factual claim because of the outcomes that would follow if it were true.
doesNotCountWhen: Consequences properly matter when choosing actions or policies, and may inform a forecast if causal evidence supports it.

fallacies.name: Appeal to desperation
fallacies.summary: Accepting a proposal because the situation is urgent, without showing that the proposal will help.
fallacies.body: A crisis can justify acting with incomplete information, but urgency does not make every available action effective or safe. The missing step is evidence that this option is better than feasible alternatives, including inaction.

examples.text: We must do something today, so approve this untested repair.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Urgency is treated as proof that a particular response is effective or justified.
doesNotCountWhen: Emergency action can be rational when delay is costly and the choice is supported by the best available risk assessment.

fallacies.name: Appeal to emotion
fallacies.summary: Relying on an emotional reaction to establish a conclusion that needs evidence or reasoning.
fallacies.body: Fear, sympathy, pride, and other feelings can draw attention to stakes; they do not establish factual premises. The defect is not emotion itself but using the reaction in place of the relevant support.

examples.text: The story is heartbreaking, so the accused must be guilty.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An emotional response is presented as the reason a factual or inferential claim should be accepted.
doesNotCountWhen: Emotion may appropriately motivate a value judgment or action when relevant facts and principles are also supplied.

fallacies.name: Appeal to equality
fallacies.summary: Treating equal treatment as requiring identical treatment despite relevant differences.
fallacies.body: Equality is a principle whose application depends on which features matter to the decision. The error assumes sameness at the surface level proves that different cases must receive the same response, or that different treatment is automatically unfair.

examples.text: All applicants must get the same test time, even though one has an approved accommodation for a disability.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A bare appeal to equality rules out a distinction without assessing whether the difference is relevant to the governing principle.
doesNotCountWhen: Equal treatment is a sound objection when the cases are alike in the respects relevant to the rule.

fallacies.name: Appeal to extremes
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a moderate position because a more extreme version of it has bad consequences.
fallacies.body: A position does not entail every stronger or more radical position nearby. This argument slides along a scale and attacks an endpoint instead of addressing the actual proposal.

examples.text: The city should reduce speeding; next it will ban all cars, so speed limits are unreasonable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An extreme consequence or position is attributed to a moderate claim without a supported chain of steps.
doesNotCountWhen: Showing that a proposal actually entails a harmful extreme through necessary intermediate steps is relevant criticism.

fallacies.name: Appeal to faith
fallacies.summary: Using faith alone as proof of a disputed factual claim for an audience that does not share that faith premise.
fallacies.body: Faith may be a source of personal commitment or a premise within a shared religious framework. The inferential gap appears when the speaker treats that commitment as independent evidence that an external claim is true.

examples.text: This herb cures infection because my faith tells me it does.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion is supported only by the speaker's faith, with no shared or independently assessable evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: An argument from religious premises can be valid within an explicitly shared framework; empirical claims still require appropriate evidence.

fallacies.name: Appeal to false authority
fallacies.summary: Using a source with no relevant expertise or an unreliable record as decisive authority for a claim.
fallacies.body: Authority matters only insofar as the source has competence in the specific field and a trustworthy basis for the statement. Status in another area, or a title alone, cannot establish the conclusion.

examples.text: A popular chef says a bridge design meets engineering standards, so it does.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The cited authority lacks relevant qualifications or reliability for the proposition and replaces substantive evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A source with relevant expertise may provide useful testimony, especially when the claim and evidence are accurately represented.

fallacies.name: Appeal to fear
fallacies.summary: Using fear of a possible harm to secure acceptance without establishing the likelihood or the proposed response's value.
fallacies.body: Risk warnings are legitimate when supported. The fallacy uses the frightening outcome itself to bypass questions about probability, causation, and whether the suggested action reduces the risk.

examples.text: If we reject this contract, the whole town could lose its jobs; sign it without review.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A fear-inducing scenario is offered as sufficient support despite missing evidence about likelihood or remedy.
doesNotCountWhen: A credible threat and an effective precaution can justify action when the risk and response are assessed.

fallacies.name: Appeal to flattery
fallacies.summary: Using praise of the audience to encourage agreement in place of reasons.
fallacies.body: Compliments can build rapport but do not make a claim true. The tactic links agreement with a flattering identity—such as being intelligent or discerning—so dissent feels like self-rejection.

examples.text: You are too perceptive to question that this investment is guaranteed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Praise or an identity reward is used as the principal reason to accept the proposition.
doesNotCountWhen: Acknowledging an audience's expertise is harmless when the argument still gives evidence they can assess.

fallacies.name: Appeal to force
fallacies.summary: Using a threat of harm or penalty to obtain agreement instead of supporting the conclusion.
fallacies.body: A threat can explain why someone complies, but compliance does not show that the proposition is true or that the demanded judgment is justified. This is also called argumentum ad baculum.

examples.text: Approve my budget or I will have you fired; therefore the budget is sound.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A threatened consequence is made the warrant for accepting a claim or judgment.
doesNotCountWhen: A lawful consequence may be relevant to practical choices, but it does not prove the associated factual claim.

fallacies.name: Appeal to heaven
fallacies.summary: Treating an unverifiable divine or supernatural endorsement as decisive proof for a disputed claim.
fallacies.body: An appeal to divine authority may be meaningful within a community that accepts its premises, but an asserted revelation does not independently settle a question for those who cannot assess that source. The issue is the unsupported inference, not religious belief itself.

examples.text: God wants this candidate to win, so the candidate's policy must work.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A claim of supernatural endorsement is used as conclusive support for a public factual or policy conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A theological conclusion can follow from premises accepted within a religious framework; empirical consequences need evidence about those consequences.

fallacies.name: Appeal to inappropriate authority
fallacies.summary: Citing an authority whose expertise does not match the subject as support for a claim.
fallacies.body: A person may be credible in one domain and uninformed in another. The argument mistakes general prestige or a real credential for competence on the particular question.

examples.text: A Nobel-winning physicist says a new tax code will increase wages, so it will.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The source's recognized authority is in an unrelated field and is doing the work of evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A qualified expert in the relevant domain can support a claim when their view is represented accurately and rests on appropriate evidence.

fallacies.name: Appeal to intuition
fallacies.summary: Treating a gut feeling as decisive evidence for a claim that needs external support.
fallacies.body: Intuition can efficiently guide judgment in familiar situations, but it may reflect bias or incomplete information. The error is treating “it feels right” as sufficient proof, especially where observations can test the claim.

examples.text: I can tell the machine is safe just by looking at it, so inspection is unnecessary.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A personal intuitive impression is the decisive warrant despite the need for evidence or expertise.
doesNotCountWhen: Intuition informed by experience can be a useful provisional signal, not an automatic conclusion.

fallacies.name: Appeal to law as proof of morality
fallacies.summary: Inferring that an action is morally right merely because the law permits it.
fallacies.body: Law and morality overlap but are not identical: laws can be unjust, incomplete, or designed for administrability rather than moral truth. Legality may matter to a practical decision without settling its ethical status.

examples.text: The company is legally allowed to dump this waste, so dumping it is morally right.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Legal permission is treated as sufficient proof of moral acceptability.
doesNotCountWhen: A legal rule can be a relevant moral consideration, but its moral force needs an argument about fairness, harm, or duties.

fallacies.name: Appeal to loyalty
fallacies.summary: Treating loyalty to a group or person as a reason to accept their claim or excuse their conduct.
fallacies.body: Commitment can support cooperation, but it does not make a factual claim accurate or misconduct acceptable. The appeal pressures the audience to choose allegiance over evaluation.

examples.text: If you are loyal to the team, you will agree the disputed result was fair.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Agreement is framed as proof of loyalty and loyalty substitutes for evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Loyalty may be a relevant value in a decision when weighed against other duties and facts; it does not verify a proposition.

fallacies.name: Appeal to motive
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a claim by alleging that its speaker has a motive, without addressing whether the claim is supported.
fallacies.body: A motive can matter when it provides evidence of bias, deception, or incentive, but motive alone does not show a proposition is false. The gap is from “they want this to be true” to “it is not true.”

examples.text: The analyst wants funding for the project, so the project's measured results must be false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An alleged motive is used as a refutation rather than as a reason to examine reliability and evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Relevant evidence of incentive can qualify a source's testimony, while leaving the claim open to independent evaluation.

fallacies.name: Appeal to nature
fallacies.summary: Assuming something is good, safe, or right simply because it is natural, or bad because it is artificial.
fallacies.body: “Natural” describes origin, not effect or value. Natural substances can be harmful and synthetic ones beneficial; the argument skips the evidence needed to connect origin with the judgment.

examples.text: This cleaner is plant-derived, so it cannot irritate skin.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Naturalness itself is offered as proof of safety, value, or moral status.
doesNotCountWhen: Natural origin can matter when a specific property of the substance is shown to affect the question.

fallacies.name: Appeal to normality
fallacies.summary: Treating what is usual or statistically typical as what is proper, healthy, or required.
fallacies.body: A frequency describes a population; it does not by itself set a standard for individuals. The inference confuses what commonly happens with what ought to happen or what is acceptable.

examples.text: Most children read by age seven, so a child who does not is necessarily lazy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A claim about what is normal is used as a sufficient reason for a normative or individual judgment.
doesNotCountWhen: A clearly stated statistical norm can support a descriptive comparison, provided it is not mistaken for a moral rule.

fallacies.name: Appeal to novelty
fallacies.summary: Treating a proposal as better or truer merely because it is new.
fallacies.body: Novelty may bring useful possibilities, but it can also bring untested risks. The argument uses recency instead of evidence about performance or accuracy.

examples.text: This is the newest battery design, so it must be safer than the old one.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Newness itself is the decisive reason for acceptance.
doesNotCountWhen: A new option can be preferred when testing or a relevant improvement supports it.

fallacies.name: Appeal to personal charm
fallacies.summary: Accepting a claim because its speaker is charming or likable rather than because it is supported.
fallacies.body: Charisma affects how a message feels, not whether its premises are true. Trustworthiness may matter to testimony, but likability alone is not a reliability check.

examples.text: The presenter is warm and confident, so her unverified forecast is accurate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's charm is the main warrant for the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A likable expert may be credible for independent reasons; charm itself does not establish the claim.

fallacies.name: Appeal to pity
fallacies.summary: Using sympathy for a person as a reason to accept an unrelated claim or excuse.
fallacies.body: Hardship deserves consideration when it bears on what response is fair. It cannot establish a factual proposition or erase a relevant standard by itself.

examples.text: Please pass my inspection; I have had a difficult month, so the equipment is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The audience's pity is used in place of evidence or a relevant justification.
doesNotCountWhen: Compassion is relevant when hardship is part of the decision criteria, but it does not prove unrelated facts.

fallacies.name: Appeal to popularity
fallacies.summary: Inferring that a claim is true or good because many people believe or choose it.
fallacies.body: Popularity measures uptake, not truth or quality. It can be relevant to preference or social convention, but not decisive evidence for a factual claim.

examples.text: Millions downloaded the app, so its privacy practices must be safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A headcount substitutes for evidence about the proposition.
doesNotCountWhen: Popularity is directly relevant when the question is what people prefer or commonly do.

fallacies.name: Appeal to possibility
fallacies.summary: Treating the mere possibility of an event as evidence that it is likely or actually happening.
fallacies.body: A scenario can be possible while remaining extremely unlikely. The inference needs evidence about probability, not merely a demonstration that the event cannot be ruled out.

examples.text: A rival could have tampered with the results, so the results are fraudulent.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument moves from “could happen” to a stronger conclusion without probability evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Possibility can justify precaution when the harm is severe and the risk is assessed, but possibility alone does not establish occurrence.

fallacies.name: Appeal to poverty
fallacies.summary: Assuming a claim is true or a person virtuous because they are poor, or false because they are wealthy.
fallacies.body: Economic status does not settle factual accuracy or moral character. Material circumstances may be relevant to interests or access, but they do not replace evaluation of the particular claim.

examples.text: The inventor had no money, so her account of the accident must be honest.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Poverty or wealth is treated as sufficient proof of truth, virtue, or deception.
doesNotCountWhen: Financial incentives can be relevant when there is evidence connecting them to the testimony, not by status alone.

fallacies.name: Appeal to probability
fallacies.summary: Treating what is probable as certain, or a possibility as proof that it occurred.
fallacies.body: Probability expresses degree of support, not certainty. The error drops that qualification and asserts a definite outcome without evidence that rules out alternatives.

examples.text: The package was probably delayed by weather, so weather definitely caused the delay.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A probabilistic premise is converted into an unconditional certainty.
doesNotCountWhen: A probability judgment can justify a calibrated conclusion such as “more likely than not” when supported by data.

fallacies.name: Appeal to ridicule
fallacies.summary: Mocking a claim or its supporter instead of answering the claim's reasons.
fallacies.body: Ridicule can make a position seem socially embarrassing, but embarrassment is not a refutation. The audience is invited to laugh rather than examine the premise or inference.

examples.text: Only a fool would believe the river data, so the flood warning is wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Mockery is used to discredit the proposition without engaging its support.
doesNotCountWhen: Humor may illustrate a genuine inconsistency, but the inconsistency—not the ridicule—must do the argumentative work.

fallacies.name: Appeal to self-evident truth
fallacies.summary: Calling a disputed proposition self-evident instead of supplying the support it needs.
fallacies.body: Some basic premises may reasonably be treated as shared starting points. The fallacy occurs when the label “obvious” conceals a contested premise or blocks requests for justification.

examples.text: It is self-evident that this tax will pay for itself, so no estimate is needed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A controversial claim is exempted from scrutiny by declaring it obvious.
doesNotCountWhen: A premise genuinely accepted by the parties and not material to the dispute may be left unstated.

fallacies.name: Appeal to spite
fallacies.summary: Supporting a choice because it will hurt or frustrate an opponent, regardless of its merits.
fallacies.body: The opponent's displeasure is not evidence that the choice is wise or just. Spite can motivate the decision while obscuring its costs to everyone, including the decision-maker.

examples.text: We should cancel the useful program because it would embarrass the rival party.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Inflicting a setback on an adversary is the main reason offered for the proposal.
doesNotCountWhen: An action that also disadvantages an opponent may still be justified by independent benefits or principles.

fallacies.name: Appeal to stupidity
fallacies.summary: Dismissing a claim by calling its supporters stupid instead of addressing their reasons.
fallacies.body: An insult about intelligence does not establish that the claim is false. Even an unreliable proponent can make a true claim, and a correct conclusion needs support beyond contempt for its source.

examples.text: Only idiots think the bridge needs repairs, so the inspection finding is wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An intelligence insult substitutes for evaluating the argument or evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A demonstrated reasoning error can be identified and explained without attacking a person's intelligence.

fallacies.name: Appeal to the moon
fallacies.summary: Using an absurd or irrelevant comparison to make a disputed claim seem ridiculous.
fallacies.body: The comparison must share features relevant to the question. An exotic analogy or remote possibility may distract from the actual evidence rather than show a real defect.

examples.text: You want a modest speed limit; next you will demand a law controlling Earth's orbit, so the limit is absurd.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A far-removed scenario is presented as if it follows from the proposal, without a relevant causal chain.
doesNotCountWhen: A comparison to an extreme case is useful when the shared features and inferential connection are demonstrated.

fallacies.name: Appeal to tradition
fallacies.summary: Treating a practice as correct merely because it has been followed for a long time.
fallacies.body: Tradition may preserve accumulated experience, but age does not establish that a practice remains effective or fair. The argument needs reasons why the practice works in the current context.

examples.text: We have always excluded renters from this committee, so the rule is fair.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Longevity itself is offered as proof of truth, value, or correctness.
doesNotCountWhen: A longstanding practice can be evidence when its continued success and relevant reasons are shown.

fallacies.name: Appeal to trust
fallacies.summary: Asking for trust as a substitute for evidence that a disputed claim is accurate.
fallacies.body: Trust can be rationally earned through a record, transparency, and accountability. A bare demand for trust asks the audience to skip those grounds and accept the speaker's assurance.

examples.text: Trust me, the accounts are correct; there is no need to inspect them.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's request for trust is the only support for a claim that can be checked.
doesNotCountWhen: Testimony from a trusted source can be reasonable when trust rests on relevant reliability and the stakes permit it.

fallacies.name: Appeal to wealth
fallacies.summary: Treating wealth as proof that a person's claim is correct or their judgment superior.
fallacies.body: Money can result from many causes and does not establish expertise or truth in a particular matter. Wealth may create relevant incentives, but status alone is not evidence.

examples.text: He is a billionaire, so his plan for public health must be correct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Financial success is used as the warrant for a claim outside what it demonstrates.
doesNotCountWhen: A wealthy person's relevant expertise and evidence can support an argument; wealth itself cannot.

fallacies.name: Argument by assertion
fallacies.summary: Repeating or forcefully stating a conclusion without providing reasons for it.
fallacies.body: An assertion can state a position, but repetition does not add support. The argument tries to make confidence or persistence stand in for the missing premises.

examples.text: The figures are fabricated. They are fabricated because I say so, and that settles it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion is merely asserted or repeated when reasons are requested.
doesNotCountWhen: A concise assertion is adequate when the claim is already supported or the exchange does not require proof.

fallacies.name: Argument by fast talking
fallacies.summary: Using speed and volume of claims to overwhelm scrutiny rather than establish the conclusion.
fallacies.body: Rapid delivery can conceal unsupported transitions, equivocations, or unanswered objections. The number and pace of statements do not strengthen each inference.

examples.text: A presenter fires off dozens of figures before anyone can check them and says the total proves the policy works.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument depends on preventing examination through pace or overload.
doesNotCountWhen: A quick summary is not fallacious when claims remain clear, supported, and open to questions.

fallacies.name: Argument by gibberish
fallacies.summary: Using incoherent or meaningless language as though it supported a conclusion.
fallacies.body: Technical-sounding words cannot establish a relation they do not express. If the key terms have no clear meaning, the audience cannot test whether the premises support the result.

examples.text: The device is effective because quantum resonance harmonizes its procedural essence.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The explanation lacks a coherent, interpretable claim while being presented as proof.
doesNotCountWhen: Unfamiliar language can be meaningful when terms are defined and the inferential steps are clear.

fallacies.name: Argument by pigheadedness
fallacies.summary: Treating refusal to reconsider as evidence that one's position is correct.
fallacies.body: Persistence is not support. A person may hold a sound conclusion firmly, but refusing every counterexample without addressing it leaves the conclusion unproven.

examples.text: I will never change my mind about the count, so my count must be right.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Stubbornness or refusal is offered as the reason the claim should prevail.
doesNotCountWhen: Maintaining a conclusion after answering objections with evidence is not this fallacy.

fallacies.name: Argument by repetition
fallacies.summary: Treating repeated exposure to a claim as if repetition made it true.
fallacies.body: Repetition can make a statement familiar and memorable, but it adds no independent evidence. The same unsupported assertion repeated many times remains unsupported.

examples.text: The product is proven safe—we have said it in every advertisement, so it is proven.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument counts repetition itself as confirmation.
doesNotCountWhen: Repeated independent measurements or sources may strengthen a claim when they provide genuinely new evidence.

fallacies.name: Argument from fallacy
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a conclusion solely because one argument offered for it is fallacious.
fallacies.body: A faulty argument fails to prove its conclusion, but that does not prove the conclusion false. The same claim may have another valid argument or independent evidence.

examples.text: That proof of the bridge's safety used an appeal to authority, so the bridge is unsafe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A defect in one supporting argument is treated as proof of the opposite conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: It is valid to say the cited argument does not establish its conclusion; a separate case is needed to refute the claim.

fallacies.name: Argument from ignorance
fallacies.summary: Treating a lack of proof for one side as proof that the opposite side is true.
fallacies.body: Not finding evidence can matter when a search would likely detect the fact if it existed. Otherwise, absence of evidence may reflect limited inquiry or weak detection, and does not automatically settle either side.

examples.text: No one has proved the file was copied, so it definitely was not copied.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion rests only on the opposing claim's lack of proof, without showing the evidence search was adequate.
doesNotCountWhen: Absence of a result can be strong evidence when a reliable, sufficiently sensitive search should have found it.

fallacies.name: Argument from inertia
fallacies.summary: Treating a current state or lack of change as a reason it should continue unchanged.
fallacies.body: The status quo may have benefits, but its persistence is not itself proof of adequacy. The argument ignores whether existing conditions meet the relevant goals or impose avoidable costs.

examples.text: The old procedure is still in place, so replacing it cannot be necessary.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The fact that a policy or state continues is offered as sufficient reason to retain it.
doesNotCountWhen: Continuity can be justified by evidence of stability, cost, or performance rather than mere existence.

fallacies.name: Argument from mystery
fallacies.summary: Using the fact that something is not understood as support for a preferred explanation.
fallacies.body: An unexplained event leaves a gap in knowledge; it does not automatically favor a supernatural, conspiratorial, or other favored account. The explanation must earn support by evidence and comparison with alternatives.

examples.text: We cannot explain this signal, so it must be a message from an extraterrestrial source.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The lack of a known explanation is treated as evidence for one selected explanation.
doesNotCountWhen: A hypothesis may be proposed to investigate an open question, provided it is not claimed proven by the gap itself.

fallacies.name: Argument from necessity
fallacies.summary: Claiming that a choice is necessary without establishing that alternatives are unavailable or inadequate.
fallacies.body: A real constraint may narrow options, but labeling a preferred choice necessary does not prove that constraint. The argument skips the comparison with feasible alternatives.

examples.text: We have to renew this vendor contract; there is no other way to keep service running.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Necessity is asserted while plausible alternatives or the supposed constraint remain unexamined.
doesNotCountWhen: A choice is genuinely necessary when relevant constraints and alternatives have been checked.

fallacies.name: Argument from omniscience
fallacies.summary: Treating lack of personal knowledge as proof that no one knows or that no evidence exists.
fallacies.body: A person's awareness is limited. The inference improperly generalizes from “I do not know” to a universal claim about what can be known or what evidence is available.

examples.text: I have never seen a study on this effect, so no study exists.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's ignorance is used to establish a universal absence of knowledge or evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A carefully bounded report of one's own knowledge is not fallacious; it simply cannot establish what everyone knows.

fallacies.name: Argument from personal incredulity
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a claim because it is difficult for the speaker to understand or imagine.
fallacies.body: Personal difficulty is not evidence of impossibility. Complex mechanisms can be real even when unfamiliar, and a plausible-sounding account can still be false; the issue requires relevant evidence.

examples.text: I cannot imagine how the species evolved that quickly, so the fossil account is false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: “I cannot see how” is treated as a refutation of a claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Pointing out that an explanation has not been made clear is appropriate when asking for evidence, not when declaring it impossible.

fallacies.name: Argument from silence
fallacies.summary: Inferring a fact from a source's failure to mention it without showing the source would have been expected to mention it.
fallacies.body: Silence is informative only when the source had reason, opportunity, and ability to record the fact. Without those conditions, omission may mean nothing.

examples.text: The inspection report does not mention a leak, so no leak existed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An omission is treated as proof without establishing that the source would likely have documented the fact.
doesNotCountWhen: Silence can count as evidence when complete reporting was expected and omissions are reliably detected.

fallacies.name: Atomistic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Drawing a conclusion about a whole system from facts about isolated parts while ignoring their interactions.
fallacies.body: Properties of components do not always combine independently. The fallacy treats pieces as though their behavior were unchanged by context, feedback, or organization.

examples.text: Each small loan is affordable, so the total set of loans must be affordable for the household.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A property of isolated parts is generalized to the whole without accounting for interactions or aggregation.
doesNotCountWhen: Adding component measures is valid when the quantity is genuinely additive and dependencies are addressed.

fallacies.name: Avoiding the issue
fallacies.summary: Responding to a related but different point while leaving the question at hand unanswered.
fallacies.body: A reply can introduce relevant context, but it avoids the issue when it changes the subject and treats that diversion as an answer. The original claim remains unaddressed.

examples.text: Asked whether the bridge passed inspection, the mayor describes the city's new parks.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response redirects from the disputed proposition without resolving or directly engaging it.
doesNotCountWhen: Adding background is not avoidance when it helps answer the actual question.

fallacies.name: Base-rate fallacy
fallacies.summary: Ignoring how common a condition or event is when interpreting a new piece of evidence about it.
fallacies.body: Evidence such as a positive test must be combined with the prior frequency of the condition and the test's accuracy. Focusing only on the vivid result can badly distort the probability of the underlying event.

examples.text: A rare disease affects 1 in 10,000 people; a test with some false positives is positive, and the patient is told they almost certainly have it without considering the base rate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The inference uses a conditional clue but omits the prior prevalence needed to estimate the target probability.
doesNotCountWhen: A base rate need not dominate when strong evidence has a very high likelihood ratio; sound inference combines both.

fallacies.name: Begging the question
fallacies.summary: Assuming the conclusion within the premises offered to prove it.
fallacies.body: The reasoning is circular: anyone who does not already accept the conclusion has not been given an independent reason to do so. The assumption can be hidden in a synonym or a premise that simply restates the point.

examples.text: This rule is fair because it is just, and we know it is just because it is fair.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The premises depend on the conclusion, directly or through an equivalent claim.
doesNotCountWhen: A premise may support the conclusion when it has independent grounds, even if the two claims are closely related.

fallacies.name: Biased sample
fallacies.summary: Drawing a population conclusion from a sample selected in a way that skews who is represented.
fallacies.body: A sample can be large yet biased if its selection systematically favors certain experiences or excludes others. The conclusion then describes the selection process more than the population.

examples.text: An online poll of a cycling club is used to claim that most residents commute by bicycle.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Who could enter or respond to the sample differs systematically from the population relevant to the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A representative sample or a clearly limited conclusion about the sampled group avoids the error.

fallacies.name: Big-lie technique
fallacies.summary: Relying on a large, repeated falsehood in the hope that its scale and confidence make it credible.
fallacies.body: The technique uses repetition and dramatic certainty to overwhelm ordinary skepticism; it provides no evidential bridge from the assertion to truth. A claim's size does not itself make it false, so the specific evidence still matters.

examples.text: A campaign repeatedly claims that thousands of ballots vanished, offering no records and dismissing every audit as part of the cover-up.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A sweeping assertion is repeated as if confidence and scale were evidence, while contrary checks are rejected without basis.
doesNotCountWhen: A broad claim supported by comprehensive evidence is not false merely because it is dramatic.

fallacies.name: Blind authority
fallacies.summary: Accepting an authority's conclusion without knowing the authority's basis, relevant competence, or possible limits.
fallacies.body: Even a qualified expert can be mistaken or speaking beyond their specialty. Deference becomes blind when the audience is asked to accept the conclusion solely on status, with no route to assess the source or reasoning.

examples.text: The committee chair says the figures are correct; no one is allowed to see the method.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Authority alone closes inquiry and the source's relevant basis cannot be assessed.
doesNotCountWhen: Provisional reliance on transparent expert consensus can be reasonable when the source is appropriately qualified and accountable.

fallacies.name: Broken-window fallacy
fallacies.summary: Counting visible spending after damage as a net economic gain while ignoring the value destroyed and alternative uses of resources.
fallacies.body: Repair work creates activity, but it replaces what was lost; it does not make the loss beneficial. The analysis must compare the actual outcome with what could have been done with the same labor and money.

examples.text: A broken shop window is said to help the economy because a glazier earns repair fees, while the shopkeeper loses money that could have bought equipment.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The claimed benefit counts replacement spending but omits the damage and forgone alternative investment.
doesNotCountWhen: Repair spending can have economic effects, but it is not evidence that causing the damage increased total welfare.

fallacies.name: Bulverism
fallacies.summary: Explaining why someone supposedly believes a claim before establishing that the claim is false.
fallacies.body: The speaker assumes the other person's conclusion is wrong, then attributes it to bias, class, or psychology. A causal account of belief does not settle the truth of what is believed.

examples.text: You support the transit plan only because you live near the proposed station, so the plan must be bad.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument substitutes a diagnosis of the believer's motive for assessing the proposition.
doesNotCountWhen: Showing a conflict of interest may affect credibility, but the claim still requires substantive evaluation.

fallacies.name: Category mistake
fallacies.summary: Applying a question or property to something that does not belong to the relevant logical category.
fallacies.body: The wording treats unlike kinds of thing as if they could answer the same question or possess the same property. Clarifying the categories often dissolves the apparent problem.

examples.text: After touring every building at the university, a visitor asks where the university itself is hidden.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A predicate or question appropriate to one category is applied literally to a different kind.
doesNotCountWhen: Metaphor or shorthand is fine when the intended category is clear and no literal inference depends on it.

fallacies.name: Causal oversimplification
fallacies.summary: Explaining a complex outcome with one factor while ignoring other important causes or conditions.
fallacies.body: A single factor can contribute without being the whole explanation. Oversimplification mistakes a partial cause for a sufficient account, which can misdirect remedies and predictions.

examples.text: Test scores fell after the school changed textbooks, so the textbook change alone caused the decline despite staffing and attendance changes.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: One cause is presented as complete without accounting for plausible contributing factors or interactions.
doesNotCountWhen: A single cause can be adequate when evidence isolates it and relevant alternatives have been ruled out.

fallacies.name: Cherry-picking
fallacies.summary: Selecting only the evidence that favors a conclusion while leaving relevant contrary evidence out of view.
fallacies.body: The selected facts may be true, yet the presentation is misleading because the omitted evidence could change the overall assessment. Selection becomes a fallacy when it distorts the evidential balance.

examples.text: A report lists three successful deployments but omits the seven failures from the same period.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The evidence is selectively sampled by outcome or direction and the omitted material is relevant to the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A focused presentation is legitimate when its scope is disclosed and it does not imply that selected evidence is the whole record.

fallacies.name: Circular definition
fallacies.summary: Defining a term with language that depends on the term itself, so the definition explains nothing independently.
fallacies.body: A useful definition should let a reader understand or identify the term without already knowing it. A circular definition simply loops back, sometimes through a synonym.

examples.text: A “reliable source” is defined as a source that can be relied on.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Understanding the definition requires presupposing the term being defined.
doesNotCountWhen: A short synonym can be adequate in a glossary when the synonym is already understood and no argument depends on it.

fallacies.name: Circular reasoning
fallacies.summary: Using a conclusion, perhaps in reworded form, as a premise for that same conclusion.
fallacies.body: The argument loops instead of providing independent support. It can sound like a chain of reasons, but each link ultimately relies on the claim it is meant to establish.

examples.text: The witness is trustworthy because she tells the truth, and we know she tells the truth because she is trustworthy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Tracing the premises reveals that they rely on the conclusion rather than independent evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A conclusion supported by independently established premises is not circular just because it later supports another claim.

fallacies.name: Circumstantial ad hominem
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a person's claim because their circumstances or interests supposedly explain why they hold it.
fallacies.body: A person's stake can signal possible bias, but it does not show their conclusion is false. The argument substitutes an account of the speaker's situation for an examination of the evidence.

examples.text: The tenant objects to the rent increase only because she pays rent, so the increase is fair.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker's circumstances are treated as a refutation of their position.
doesNotCountWhen: A specific conflict can be relevant to weighing testimony, but the merits and independent evidence still matter.

fallacies.name: Commutation of conditionals
fallacies.summary: Treating “if A then B” as equivalent to “if B then A.”
fallacies.body: A conditional guarantees the consequent when its antecedent holds; it does not say the consequent can occur only that way. Reversing the direction silently turns a sufficient condition into a necessary one.

examples.text: If a device is charging, its indicator is lit; the indicator is lit, so the device is charging.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument reverses a conditional without a premise that makes it biconditional.
doesNotCountWhen: The reverse follows when an independent premise establishes that B occurs only if A.

fallacies.name: Complex question
fallacies.summary: Asking a question that presupposes a disputed claim, forcing an answer to accept that assumption.
fallacies.body: A yes-or-no answer may appear to concede a premise that has not been established. The question must be separated into its presupposition and the point actually being asked.

examples.text: Have you stopped falsifying the maintenance logs?

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The question embeds a contested assumption that either direct answer would appear to grant.
doesNotCountWhen: A question is fair when its presupposition is established or the respondent can challenge it without being framed as evasive.

fallacies.name: Composition fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming that what is true of each part must also be true of the whole.
fallacies.body: Parts can combine in ways that change a property: what works for one component may fail at scale or in a group. The inference needs a reason that the property carries over.

examples.text: Each player is an excellent solo performer, so the team must play well together.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A property of individual members is attributed to the aggregate without showing it is preserved under combination.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is sound for properties that genuinely distribute across the whole, such as each member being present in the set.

fallacies.name: Conflicting conditions
fallacies.summary: Requiring conditions that cannot all be satisfied, then treating failure as a defect in the person or proposal.
fallacies.body: The standards conflict when meeting one necessarily violates another. The resulting failure does not show lack of effort or merit; it shows that the requirements need reconciliation.

examples.text: A job requires five years of experience and accepts only applicants graduating this year.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The stated criteria cannot jointly be met, yet compliance is demanded as if they were compatible.
doesNotCountWhen: Multiple demanding criteria are not conflicting when a candidate can satisfy them together.

fallacies.name: Confusing explanation with excuse
fallacies.summary: Treating an explanation of why conduct occurred as if it excused or justified the conduct.
fallacies.body: Causal explanation answers how or why an event happened; excuse concerns responsibility, and justification concerns whether it was permissible. These questions can overlap but do not collapse into one another.

examples.text: The driver was exhausted, so the crash-causing decision to ignore the warning was acceptable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A cause or motive is treated as sufficient moral justification or excuse without addressing the relevant standard.
doesNotCountWhen: An explanation may support an excuse when it establishes a recognized factor such as coercion or incapacity.

fallacies.name: Confusing unexplained with unexplainable
fallacies.summary: Inferring that an event can never be explained because no explanation is currently known.
fallacies.body: Current ignorance is a limit on available knowledge, not a proof about what can be known in principle. The argument turns a temporary gap into an absolute impossibility.

examples.text: Scientists have not identified the signal's source, so the signal is unexplainable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A lack of present explanation is generalized into a claim that explanation is impossible.
doesNotCountWhen: A claim of unexplainability can be argued from principled limits, but not from present lack of an answer alone.

fallacies.name: Conjunction fallacy
fallacies.summary: Judging a detailed combination of events more likely than one event it includes.
fallacies.body: A conjunction cannot be more probable than either of its components because every case in which both occur is also a case in which each one occurs. A vivid description can make the narrower combination feel more representative, but feeling is not probability.

examples.text: A person is judged more likely to be a nurse and an activist than simply a nurse because the description fits the stereotype.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The probability assigned to A-and-B exceeds the probability assigned to A or B alone.
doesNotCountWhen: A conjunction can be more informative or plausible in ordinary speech; the fallacy concerns probability judgments.

fallacies.name: Continuum fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming that because a boundary is vague, no meaningful distinction can be made.
fallacies.body: Some categories have borderline cases, but a fuzzy edge does not erase clear cases or prevent practical thresholds. The argument wrongly demands a perfectly sharp boundary before using a category at all.

examples.text: There is no exact moment when a pile becomes a heap, so nothing can ever count as a heap.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Borderline cases are used to deny that the category has any valid applications.
doesNotCountWhen: Acknowledging that a cutoff is conventional or uncertain is not denying the usefulness of the category.

fallacies.name: Converse accident
fallacies.summary: Generalizing from an unusual case to a broad rule for ordinary cases.
fallacies.body: A rare or exceptional example may not represent the population. The inference ignores how the case differs and assumes the same outcome will occur generally.

examples.text: One person recovered without treatment, so patients generally do not need treatment.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An exceptional instance is used as representative evidence for a general conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A single case can establish possibility or motivate study without supporting a population-wide rule.

fallacies.name: Correlation implies causation
fallacies.summary: Inferring that one variable causes another merely because they change together.
fallacies.body: Correlation may arise because A causes B, B causes A, a third factor affects both, or the association is coincidental. Establishing causation requires evidence that distinguishes these possibilities.

examples.text: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise in summer, so ice cream causes drownings.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An observed association is treated as a causal effect without ruling out reverse direction, common causes, or coincidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Correlation is relevant causal evidence when combined with design, timing, mechanism, or controls that support the causal interpretation.

fallacies.name: Defense attorney's fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating the possibility of doubt about each piece of evidence as proof that the overall case is weak or false.
fallacies.body: A standard of proof may require addressing reasonable doubt, but merely imagining a remote alternative does not make it reasonable. The argument discounts cumulative evidence by scrutinizing each item in isolation and demanding certainty.

examples.text: Each witness might be mistaken, so the consistent records and testimony together prove nothing.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Speculative alternatives are used to dismiss converging evidence without showing they are plausible.
doesNotCountWhen: A specific, evidence-based doubt about a key link is relevant and can materially weaken a case.

fallacies.name: Definist fallacy
fallacies.summary: Defining a disputed term in a loaded way that builds the desired judgment into the definition.
fallacies.body: Definitions can clarify language, but a slanted definition smuggles an evaluation into what appears to be a neutral description. The argument then seems to prove the evaluation by definition.

examples.text: A “real patriot” is defined as someone who supports this bill; dissenters are dismissed as unpatriotic.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A definition is tailored to settle the disputed issue by assigning a favorable or unfavorable label.
doesNotCountWhen: A stipulative definition is acceptable when announced clearly and not treated as evidence that the underlying value judgment is true.

fallacies.name: Denying a conjunct
fallacies.summary: In logic, inferring that one part of a conjunction is false from the fact that the whole conjunction is false.
fallacies.body: From not-(A and B), it follows only that at least one of A or B fails; it does not identify which one. The argument overstates what the denial establishes.

examples.text: The report is not both accurate and complete; therefore it is inaccurate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A denial of a conjunction is used to deny one specific conjunct without additional information.
doesNotCountWhen: The conclusion follows if another premise establishes that the other conjunct is true.

fallacies.name: Denying the antecedent
fallacies.summary: Inferring that a result will not occur because one sufficient route to it did not occur.
