fallacies.body: The form is: if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q. P may be sufficient for Q without being the only cause, so Q may still happen by another route.

examples.text: If the heater is on, the room warms; the heater is off, so the room cannot warm.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument denies the antecedent and then denies the consequent of a one-way conditional.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is valid if the conditional is a biconditional or other causes of Q are excluded.

fallacies.name: Denying the correlative
fallacies.summary: Assuming that rejecting one side of a relationship removes the other side as well.
fallacies.body: Correlative roles or concepts can depend on one another, but denying one person's role does not automatically establish that the other role is absent. The terms and relationship need to be analyzed rather than treated as a single package.

examples.text: There is no employer here, so none of these people can be employees.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument denies one related role and concludes the paired role cannot exist without establishing that dependency.
doesNotCountWhen: If a term is defined strictly by its reciprocal relation, evidence that one side is absent may rule out the other.

fallacies.name: Disjunction fallacy
fallacies.summary: Inferring that neither option is true from a disjunction that says at least one must be true.
fallacies.body: A true inclusive “A or B” guarantees at least one disjunct. Concluding not-A and not-B contradicts that premise unless the wording or context establishes another interpretation.

examples.text: The key is either in the drawer or in the cabinet; it is not in the drawer, so it is not in the cabinet.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reasoning rejects both disjuncts despite an inclusive premise asserting at least one.
doesNotCountWhen: The conclusion may follow if the original statement was mistaken or if neither option was exhaustive; those require separate evidence.

fallacies.name: Distinction without a difference
fallacies.summary: Drawing a distinction between cases that does not affect the question being decided.
fallacies.body: Different wording or labels do not establish a meaningful difference. A distinction matters only if the cited feature changes the relevant evidence, rule, or consequence.

examples.text: The company says the payment is a “processing contribution,” not a fee, though customers pay it for the same service.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A verbal or superficial distinction is used to avoid a conclusion while no relevant difference is identified.
doesNotCountWhen: A distinction is valid when the difference has a demonstrated bearing on the issue.

fallacies.name: Division fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming that what is true of a whole must be true of each part or member.
fallacies.body: Aggregate properties need not distribute to individuals. A wealthy organization may contain low-paid workers; a large object may be heavy while each component is light.

examples.text: The company made a large profit, so every employee must be wealthy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A property of a group or whole is assigned to every component without a distribution rule.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is valid for properties that apply to every member by definition or evidence.

fallacies.name: Dog-whistle argument
fallacies.summary: Using coded wording that signals one meaning to a target audience while retaining a more innocent public reading.
fallacies.body: The ambiguity can let a speaker mobilize an in-group response while denying the implication to others. Identifying a dog whistle requires context and evidence of the intended coded meaning, not merely suspicion about a phrase.

examples.text: A candidate repeatedly invokes “taking our country back” to signal exclusion to supporters while claiming it means only administrative reform.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A phrase has a contextually supported coded message, and the speaker exploits its dual audience meanings to avoid direct argument.
doesNotCountWhen: A phrase with multiple meanings is not automatically a dog whistle; context may support a straightforward, non-coded use.

fallacies.name: Double standard
fallacies.summary: Applying different standards to comparable cases without a relevant reason for the difference.
fallacies.body: Different outcomes can be fair when cases differ in a way that matters. The fallacy is inconsistency: the same evidential or moral rule is tightened for one side and relaxed for another.

examples.text: A manager demands documentation from one team but accepts an unsupported verbal claim from another in the same review.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Comparable cases receive different standards and no relevant distinction explains the disparity.
doesNotCountWhen: Different treatment is justified when a relevant difference, such as risk or responsibility, warrants it.

fallacies.name: Ecological fallacy
fallacies.summary: Inferring facts about individuals from group-level statistics.
fallacies.body: An association between groups does not necessarily hold for each member; within-group patterns can differ or even reverse. Aggregated data answer population questions, not automatically individual ones.

examples.text: A district has a high average income, so a particular resident must be wealthy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A group average or relationship is attributed to an individual without individual-level evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: Group statistics can inform an individual probability when the population fit and uncertainty are stated; they do not determine that individual's case.

fallacies.name: Equivocation
fallacies.summary: Shifting the meaning of a key word during an argument so the conclusion appears to follow.
fallacies.body: The premises and conclusion may each sound plausible, but they use the same word in different senses. The reasoning fails because the apparent shared term conceals a change in meaning.

examples.text: The sign says “fine for parking”; anything fine is acceptable; therefore parking here is acceptable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A central term changes sense between premises and conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A word may have several meanings without error when the argument uses one consistent sense throughout.

fallacies.name: Etymological fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming a word's present meaning must match its historical roots.
fallacies.body: Word origins explain linguistic history, not current usage. Meaning changes over time and is established by contemporary convention and context, not by breaking a word into older parts.

examples.text: “Decimate” cannot mean destroy most of something because its Latin root referred to one in ten.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A historical derivation is treated as decisive evidence about current meaning.
doesNotCountWhen: Etymology is relevant when discussing a word's history or a context that deliberately invokes its original sense.

fallacies.name: Every-and-all fallacy
fallacies.summary: Confusing a claim about each member or each occasion with a claim about the whole set or every possible case.
fallacies.body: Quantifiers have precise scope. “Each person did one task” does not mean each person did every task; “all members are represented” does not mean every possible member is present. The argument changes the quantifier's reach.

examples.text: Every committee member reviewed a section, so every member reviewed every section.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reasoning shifts between distributive and collective or universal readings of “every” and “all.”
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is sound when the stated quantifier genuinely covers the same items and scope in both claims.

fallacies.name: Exclusive premises
fallacies.summary: In categorical logic, drawing a conclusion from two negative premises even though neither links the terms.
fallacies.body: Two exclusion statements can show that each group lies outside a third category, but they do not establish how the first two groups relate to each other. The conclusion introduces a connection the premises never provide.

examples.text: No cats are reptiles; no dogs are reptiles; therefore no cats are dogs.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Both premises are negative, leaving no valid shared middle relation to support the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A conclusion may follow if an additional affirmative premise relates the subject and predicate.

fallacies.name: Existential fallacy
fallacies.summary: Inferring that a class has members when the premises only describe a relationship among classes.
fallacies.body: A universal statement such as “all unicorns are imaginary” does not assert that unicorns exist. Treating it as existential adds a claim absent from the premises.

examples.text: All dragons are fictional; therefore some dragons are fictional.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument derives an existential conclusion from universal premises without establishing that the subject class has members.
doesNotCountWhen: Existence follows when a premise explicitly asserts at least one member or the logic system includes an existence assumption.

fallacies.name: Fact-to-fiction fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating a fact, observation, or prediction as though it were a fictional or invented account, or vice versa, without a basis for the shift.
fallacies.body: The label blurs the boundary between evidence and narrative: a true event can be dramatized, and a plausible story can still be invented. The argument must assess documentation rather than infer status from how the account feels.

examples.text: The incident sounds unbelievable, so the recorded witness accounts must be fiction.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The factual status of an account is inferred from its narrative quality rather than its evidence or provenance.
doesNotCountWhen: Calling out a demonstrable fabrication or identifying fictional framing is valid when supported by source evidence.

fallacies.name: Failure to elucidate
fallacies.summary: Offering an explanation that uses unclear terms or leaves the crucial mechanism unexplained.
fallacies.body: An explanation should make the phenomenon more understandable. Repeating the claim in technical language, or introducing undefined causes, merely renames the gap rather than filling it.

examples.text: The software crashed because of an anomalous semantic instability in its execution essence.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The purported explanation does not clarify the cause or provide terms that can be checked.
doesNotCountWhen: A brief explanation can be adequate when its key mechanism is already understood in context.

fallacies.name: False analogy
fallacies.summary: Drawing a conclusion from a comparison that overlooks differences relevant to the conclusion.
fallacies.body: Analogies support an inference only when the shared features bear on the property being inferred. Similarity in one respect does not show the cases will behave alike in another.

examples.text: A city is like a household, so it should balance its budget each year in the same way a family does.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The analogy relies on similarities that do not establish the transferred conclusion, while material differences go unanswered.
doesNotCountWhen: An analogy is useful when its relevant similarities and limits are made explicit.

fallacies.name: False attribution
fallacies.summary: Assigning a statement, action, or source to the wrong person or group.
fallacies.body: A claim's apparent support can be manufactured by misidentifying who said it or what they endorsed. Attribution needs a traceable source and context; repetition does not verify it.

examples.text: A post attributes a fabricated quotation to the mayor and uses it to claim the mayor supports the plan.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument depends on an attribution that lacks reliable provenance or conflicts with the source context.
doesNotCountWhen: Attribution is reasonable when supported by a reliable recording, document, or corroborated report.

fallacies.name: False balance
fallacies.summary: Presenting opposing positions as equally supported when the evidence is substantially stronger on one side.
fallacies.body: Fairness does not require equal weight for unequal evidence. Giving a fringe or weakly supported view the same standing as a well-established conclusion distorts the audience's picture of the evidence.

examples.text: A report gives equal time to a large body of safety research and one unsupported claim of harm, implying scientific parity.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The presentation implies evidential equality despite a clear difference in quality, quantity, or expert support.
doesNotCountWhen: Representing genuine uncertainty or a live expert disagreement fairly is not false balance.

fallacies.name: False cause
fallacies.summary: Assigning a causal relationship without adequate evidence that one event produced the other.
fallacies.body: The label covers causal errors such as confusing sequence with causation or ignoring common causes. A plausible story about mechanism is not enough; the evidence must distinguish it from alternatives.

examples.text: The new sign was installed, then accidents fell, so the sign caused the decline, though traffic also dropped sharply.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A causal conclusion outruns the temporal or correlational evidence and ignores plausible alternatives.
doesNotCountWhen: Causal claims are reasonable when supported by a design or converging evidence that addresses alternatives.

fallacies.name: False dilemma
fallacies.summary: Presenting two choices as the only possibilities when additional options exist.
fallacies.body: A forced either/or narrows debate and makes one option seem inevitable. The argument is defective when the alternatives are not exhaustive or mutually exclusive as claimed.

examples.text: Either approve this expensive contract today or accept that the service will shut down.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument's choice set omits plausible alternatives relevant to the decision.
doesNotCountWhen: A two-option framing is sound when the options really are exhaustive and the distinction is clear.

fallacies.name: False effect
fallacies.summary: Claiming that an alleged cause must have a particular effect without evidence for that causal link.
fallacies.body: The existence of a cause does not guarantee a predicted consequence; effects may depend on context, magnitude, or countervailing factors. The inference treats a possible effect as automatic.

examples.text: A small tax cut will necessarily create enough growth to pay for itself.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument asserts an effect as inevitable from a proposed cause without support for the mechanism or conditions.
doesNotCountWhen: A causal effect can be predicted when evidence establishes the mechanism and relevant conditions.

fallacies.name: False equivalence
fallacies.summary: Treating two things as equivalent despite differences that matter to the comparison.
fallacies.body: A shared label or one similarity does not erase differences in scale, evidence, responsibility, or consequence. The comparison must specify which dimension is being equated and why.

examples.text: A delayed library book and a stolen car are called equally serious because both involve property.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats unlike cases as equal on a relevant judgment without a defensible comparison basis.
doesNotCountWhen: Equivalence is appropriate when the cases match on the dimensions relevant to the question.

fallacies.name: False precision
fallacies.summary: Giving a number more exactness than the measurement or evidence supports.
fallacies.body: Extra decimal places can make an estimate look authoritative without reducing uncertainty. Precision is not accuracy, and a reported figure should reflect how it was measured.

examples.text: A rough survey estimate is reported as 63.847 percent despite a small, uncertain sample.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The numerical specificity exceeds the instrument, sampling, or method's justified resolution.
doesNotCountWhen: Exact figures are appropriate when the underlying measurement genuinely supports that precision.

fallacies.name: False trilemma
fallacies.summary: Claiming there are exactly three choices when the alternatives are incomplete or not mutually exclusive.
fallacies.body: A trilemma is a three-way version of a false dilemma. The count of options is not evidence that the list is exhaustive, and alternatives may overlap.

examples.text: You can either quit, accept the cut, or transfer; the employer omits negotiating or seeking another role.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Three options are presented as exhaustive without establishing that no others exist.
doesNotCountWhen: A three-way classification is valid when the categories are exhaustive and distinct for the decision.

fallacies.name: Fantasy projection
fallacies.summary: Treating an imagined scenario or desired future as if it were evidence about what will happen.
fallacies.body: Speculation can help explore possibilities, but it does not establish probability. The argument mistakes vividness or personal vision for evidence about real-world constraints and outcomes.

examples.text: I can picture the company expanding worldwide, so the expansion is certain to succeed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An imagined scenario is used as factual support without evidence connecting it to likely outcomes.
doesNotCountWhen: Scenario planning is useful when possibilities are labeled as such and tested against evidence.

fallacies.name: Far-fetched hypothesis
fallacies.summary: Preferring an unlikely, unsupported explanation over a simpler account without evidence that warrants it.
fallacies.body: An unusual hypothesis is not false merely because it is unusual, but its extra assumptions require support. The error is selecting it despite weaker fit and no reason to discount ordinary explanations.

examples.text: The missing parcel was likely teleported away rather than misdelivered, though no evidence supports teleportation.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A highly improbable explanation is accepted without comparative evidence or a need it uniquely explains.
doesNotCountWhen: A surprising hypothesis is justified when strong evidence favors it over ordinary alternatives.

fallacies.name: Faulty comparison
fallacies.summary: Drawing a conclusion from a comparison that uses mismatched measures, groups, or conditions.
fallacies.body: Comparisons need like-for-like definitions and contexts. A difference can be an artifact of who was counted, the time period, or the metric rather than a real performance difference.

examples.text: This school is declared worse because its raw incident count exceeds a smaller school's count, without adjusting for enrollment.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The compared quantities differ in a way that undermines the claimed inference.
doesNotCountWhen: A comparison is informative when relevant denominators, periods, and conditions are aligned.

fallacies.name: Faulty inductive conversion
fallacies.summary: Reversing an inductive relationship and assuming the same probability applies in the opposite direction.
fallacies.body: A group may have a high rate of a trait without most people who show the trait belonging to that group. The reversed conditional ignores the size and prevalence of each group.

examples.text: Most people with a condition test positive, so most positive tests must come from people with the condition.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A probability such as P(result|condition) is treated as if it established P(condition|result).
doesNotCountWhen: Reversal is warranted when the relevant base rates and conditional probabilities support it.

fallacies.name: Feedback fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating feedback as proof of success without checking who responded, what it measures, or how it relates to the outcome.
fallacies.body: Feedback can reveal experience, but favorable comments may come from a self-selected group or measure satisfaction rather than effectiveness. The inference needs a representative process and a metric tied to the claim.

examples.text: A few enthusiastic users praise the course, so it demonstrably improved learning for all students.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Feedback is generalized beyond its respondents or treated as a direct measure of an outcome it did not assess.
doesNotCountWhen: Representative feedback using a relevant measure can support claims about user experience or results.

fallacies.name: Fixed-pie fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming that one person's gain must be another person's equal loss when the total can change or expand.
fallacies.body: Some resources are fixed in a particular decision, but many exchanges create value or alter the size of the available pool. The error assumes a zero-sum relationship without establishing it.

examples.text: If one department receives a training budget, another department must lose the same amount in productivity.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A conflict is treated as zero-sum despite possible gains, substitutes, or a changing total.
doesNotCountWhen: A fixed budget or scarce indivisible resource can make a particular allocation genuinely zero-sum.

fallacies.name: Four-term fallacy
fallacies.summary: Using a middle term in two different senses, so a syllogism appears to connect its subject and predicate when it does not.
fallacies.body: A categorical syllogism needs exactly one shared middle category. If the middle word shifts meaning, the premises concern different things and no valid link is established.

examples.text: All banks hold money; river banks hold soil; therefore river banks hold money.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The apparent middle term changes meaning across the two premises.
doesNotCountWhen: A syllogism is sound when the middle term retains one precise sense and the categorical form is valid.

fallacies.name: Furtive fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming that a hidden or deliberate cause must explain an outcome merely because the cause is not obvious.
fallacies.body: The argument treats lack of visible evidence as a sign of concealment, then uses that supposed concealment to protect the theory. A secret cause needs positive evidence, not just invisibility.

examples.text: The records show no coordination, which proves the group concealed its coordination perfectly.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Absence of evidence is reinterpreted as evidence of a covert explanation without independent support.
doesNotCountWhen: A hidden cause can be real when there is positive evidence of concealment or its effects.

fallacies.name: Gadarene-swine fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating a crowd's collective movement or behavior as proof that its members are right or that a bad outcome is inevitable.
fallacies.body: A group may move together through imitation, pressure, or shared incentives. The spectacle of many people acting alike does not establish the truth of their belief or prove that others must follow.

examples.text: Every firm in the sector is adopting this software, so our firm must adopt it too.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Collective momentum is treated as evidence of correctness or inevitability.
doesNotCountWhen: A widespread choice can be informative when independent decision-makers respond to relevant evidence, but the reasons still matter.

fallacies.name: Galileo fallacy
fallacies.summary: Claiming that rejection by authorities or a majority proves a person's idea is correct, by comparing them to a persecuted pioneer.
fallacies.body: A true idea can face resistance, but most rejected ideas are not thereby vindicated. The historical analogy supplies no evidence for the present claim and encourages the speaker to treat criticism as confirmation.

examples.text: Scientists dispute my unsupported theory, just as they once opposed Galileo, so I must be right.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Being criticized or outnumbered is presented as evidence that the claim is true.
doesNotCountWhen: A minority view can be correct when supported by evidence; its minority status alone neither confirms nor refutes it.

fallacies.name: Gambler's fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming that a random outcome is due to reverse itself because one outcome has occurred repeatedly.
fallacies.body: For independent trials, past results do not change the probability of the next one. A sequence can look unbalanced by chance, and randomness does not guarantee short-term alternation.

examples.text: A fair coin landed heads five times, so tails is now more likely on the next toss.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The prediction treats independent outcomes as if past streaks changed the next trial's odds.
doesNotCountWhen: Past outcomes matter when trials are dependent or the process is not actually fair and independent.

fallacies.name: Genetic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Judging a claim by where it came from rather than by its present evidence or merits.
fallacies.body: Origins can matter if they reveal a relevant bias or reliability problem, but they do not automatically make a proposition false or true. The argument substitutes provenance for evaluation.

examples.text: The safety report came from an industry group, so every finding in it is false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The source or history of the claim is treated as sufficient proof of its truth or falsity.
doesNotCountWhen: Provenance is relevant to evidential weight when linked to methods, incentives, or reliability and then assessed alongside the evidence.

fallacies.name: Gish gallop
fallacies.summary: Flooding a discussion with many rapid claims so opponents cannot answer each one in the available time.
fallacies.body: The tactic exploits an imbalance between making claims and checking them. A large pile of assertions does not become strong evidence; each claim needs support, and unanswered claims are not thereby conceded.

examples.text: A speaker lists twenty alleged defects in a study during a short debate, then says no response proves the study is invalid.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The volume and pace of claims overwhelm examination, and lack of immediate rebuttal is treated as confirmation.
doesNotCountWhen: Presenting many well-supported points is not a gish gallop when they are organized and given fair time for response.

fallacies.name: Guilt by association
fallacies.summary: Discrediting a person or claim solely because of an association with a disliked person or group.
fallacies.body: Association does not transfer guilt or make a proposition false. A connection matters only when evidence shows involvement, shared conduct, or a relevant influence.

examples.text: The researcher once worked with a disgraced executive, so her measurements are fraudulent.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A negative association is used as a substitute for evidence about the person or claim.
doesNotCountWhen: A documented collaboration or shared action can be relevant when it directly bears on responsibility or reliability.

fallacies.name: Hasty generalization
fallacies.summary: Drawing a broad rule from too few or unrepresentative examples.
fallacies.body: A small set of cases may not capture the variation in the population. The generalization outruns its sample, especially when cases were chosen because they are memorable or convenient.

examples.text: Two delayed trains show that the entire rail network is unreliable.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion covers a broader population or pattern than the observations can represent.
doesNotCountWhen: A modest conclusion limited to the observed cases is valid; broader estimates need an adequate sample.

fallacies.name: Having your cake
fallacies.summary: Claiming incompatible benefits can both be kept without acknowledging the trade-off or mechanism needed.
fallacies.body: Some apparent conflicts can be resolved creatively, but the speaker must show how. The fallacy assumes mutually exclusive outcomes can coexist merely because both are wanted.

examples.text: The firm will cut staff costs while keeping every role and reducing nobody's workload.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The proposal promises incompatible outcomes while ignoring the constraint connecting them.
doesNotCountWhen: Both aims may be achievable when a concrete efficiency or resource change reconciles them.

fallacies.name: Hedging
fallacies.summary: Using vague qualifications to avoid commitment while presenting the claim as if it were informative or decisive.
fallacies.body: Words like “perhaps,” “some,” or “in a sense” can accurately express uncertainty. Hedging becomes evasive when the claim is shifted after challenge so that no clear proposition can be tested.

examples.text: The forecast says the policy may possibly have some effect, then later claims it predicted the exact outcome.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Qualifications are manipulated to claim credit while avoiding a definite, assessable prediction.
doesNotCountWhen: Calibrated uncertainty is responsible when the claim's scope and confidence are stated consistently.

fallacies.name: Heroes-all fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming a group consists entirely of heroic or exemplary members because a few celebrated members are highlighted.
fallacies.body: Praise for selected individuals does not establish the character or conduct of everyone in the group. The inference generalizes from exceptional examples while overlooking ordinary variation.

examples.text: Several decorated officers acted bravely, so misconduct allegations against the department cannot be true.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Selected heroes are used to shield the whole group from criticism or scrutiny.
doesNotCountWhen: Examples of exemplary conduct can support claims about those individuals, not universal claims about the group.

fallacies.name: Historian's fallacy
fallacies.summary: Judging past actors as if they knew what later observers know, or using hindsight to treat an outcome as obvious.
fallacies.body: Historical decisions must be assessed against information and options available at the time. Knowing what happened later can make uncertain choices look inevitable or foolish when they were not.

examples.text: The officials should have predicted the collapse because we now know the warning signs that became clear afterward.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The evaluation imports later knowledge into the actor's earlier information set.
doesNotCountWhen: Criticism is fair when contemporaneous evidence shows the actor could reasonably have recognized the risk.

fallacies.name: Hollow man
fallacies.summary: Replacing an opponent's position with an empty, vague, or distorted version that is easier to dismiss.
fallacies.body: A hollowed-out claim strips away the opponent's actual qualifications or reasons. Refuting that version does not answer the position they defended.

examples.text: The proposal is to phase out one obsolete rule; the reply attacks the vague idea of abolishing all rules.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response targets a weaker or less precise formulation than the opponent actually advanced.
doesNotCountWhen: Summarizing a position briefly is fair when it preserves the material claims and qualifications.

fallacies.name: Homunculus fallacy
fallacies.summary: Explaining a process by inserting a smaller inner agent that performs the same unexplained process.
fallacies.body: The explanation relocates the question rather than answering it: if an inner observer interprets information, the account must still explain how that observer does so. Repeating the mechanism at a smaller scale adds no explanatory power.

examples.text: Vision works because a tiny person inside the brain watches the images and understands them.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The proposed explanation reproduces the original problem inside an imagined inner agent.
doesNotCountWhen: A model of distinct processing stages is useful when each stage has an independently specified mechanism, not a miniature duplicate person.

fallacies.name: Honor by association
fallacies.summary: Treating a claim as more credible because it is associated with a respected person or group.
fallacies.body: Admiration does not transfer evidential support from one person's reputation to another's proposition. The connection must be relevant to the claim and its evidence.

examples.text: A respected scientist once attended this conference, so the conference's health claims are trustworthy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A positive association is used to confer credibility without showing expertise or evidential contribution.
doesNotCountWhen: A named expert's direct, relevant, and supported endorsement can count as testimony.

fallacies.name: Hot-hand fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming a person is more likely to succeed next because of a recent streak, without evidence that the streak predicts future performance.
fallacies.body: A run of successes may be random, or it may reflect a real change in skill or conditions. The fallacy assumes momentum from the streak alone rather than testing whether outcomes are dependent.

examples.text: A shooter made several independent long shots, so the next shot is automatically more likely to go in.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A recent streak is treated as predictive without evidence of a changed underlying probability.
doesNotCountWhen: A hot-hand effect is possible when data show performance is serially dependent or conditions have changed.

fallacies.name: Hypnotic bait-and-switch
fallacies.summary: Drawing attention with one claim or promise, then quietly replacing it with a different, weaker one.
fallacies.body: The audience is attracted by the initial proposition, while the argument later defends a substitute. Because the two claims differ, support for the substitute does not fulfill the original promise.

examples.text: An ad promises a “secure system,” then after a breach says it meant only that passwords were encrypted in transit.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The defended claim shifts after attention or commitment has been secured, without acknowledging the change.
doesNotCountWhen: Clarifying a genuinely ambiguous claim is fair when the revision is explicit and the original is not misrepresented.

fallacies.name: Identity fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating someone's group identity as proof that their claim is true or false.
fallacies.body: Identity can shape experience and can be relevant to whose perspective is represented. It does not automatically settle a factual claim; the evidence and reasoning still need examination.

examples.text: She belongs to the affected community, so every factual claim she makes about the project is correct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Identity is used as a substitute for evidence or as an automatic disqualification.
doesNotCountWhen: Lived experience is relevant evidence about that person's experience and may inform broader inquiry, with suitable limits.

fallacies.name: If-by-whiskey
fallacies.summary: Using deliberately ambiguous language so either audience reaction can be claimed as agreement.
fallacies.body: The speaker's wording is constructed to sound favorable to different listeners for incompatible reasons. It avoids stating a clear position that could be evaluated.

examples.text: The mayor praises the “necessary and avoidable” fee, allowing supporters to hear support and opponents to hear rejection.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The statement's ambiguity is strategically used to imply incompatible commitments to different audiences.
doesNotCountWhen: A nuanced statement is not this tactic when its qualifications clarify a consistent position.

fallacies.name: Ignoratio elenchi
fallacies.summary: Offering reasons that may support a point but do not establish the conclusion actually at issue.
fallacies.body: The argument can be valid in its own direction yet irrelevant to the question. It proves a nearby proposition, leaving the target proposition untouched; this is often called an irrelevant conclusion.

examples.text: Asked whether the plan meets safety standards, the spokesperson explains that it creates jobs.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The premises support a different conclusion from the one the dispute requires.
doesNotCountWhen: A related benefit is relevant when the question is whether to adopt the plan overall, but it does not answer a separate safety claim.

fallacies.name: Ignoring a common cause
fallacies.summary: Treating two correlated events as directly causal while overlooking a third factor that could produce both.
fallacies.body: A common cause can create an association without either observed variable causing the other. The causal account must consider shared drivers such as season, policy, or population change.

examples.text: Umbrella sales and traffic accidents rise together; rain may increase both, rather than umbrellas causing crashes.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The explanation overlooks a plausible shared cause of the association.
doesNotCountWhen: A direct causal link can still exist if evidence distinguishes it from common-cause explanations.

fallacies.name: Illicit contraposition
fallacies.summary: In categorical logic, reversing and negating a statement in a way its form does not permit.
fallacies.body: Contraposition is valid for some categorical forms but not all. For example, “all A are B” supports “all non-B are non-A,” while “some A are B” does not support “some non-B are non-A.” The conversion depends on quantifier and quality.

examples.text: Some birds are pets; therefore some things that are not pets are not birds.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument applies contraposition to a categorical proposition whose form does not preserve truth.
doesNotCountWhen: Contraposition is valid when the statement type permits it, such as a universal affirmative under standard categorical logic.

fallacies.name: Illicit conversion
fallacies.summary: Reversing a categorical statement's subject and predicate when that form does not allow reversal.
fallacies.body: “All A are B” does not mean “all B are A”; inclusion in one direction does not establish equal membership. Some forms, such as “no A are B,” can be converted validly.

examples.text: All nurses are trained; therefore all trained people are nurses.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The subject and predicate are swapped without a valid conversion rule.
doesNotCountWhen: Conversion is valid for forms whose relation is symmetric, such as “no A are B” or “some A are B.”

fallacies.name: Illicit major
fallacies.summary: In a categorical syllogism, distributing the major term in the conclusion when it was not distributed in the premise.
fallacies.body: The conclusion makes a claim about the entire predicate class, but the premise only spoke about part of that class. It therefore reaches beyond the scope of its support.

examples.text: All cats are mammals; no dogs are cats; therefore no dogs are mammals.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The major term is universal in the conclusion but not covered universally in the corresponding premise.
doesNotCountWhen: The syllogism is valid if the major premise distributes the term as widely as the conclusion does.

fallacies.name: Illicit minor
fallacies.summary: In a categorical syllogism, distributing the minor term in the conclusion when the premise did not cover it universally.
fallacies.body: The conclusion makes a universal claim about the subject class, although the premise only concerned some members. The term's scope expands without support.

examples.text: All cats are mammals; some pets are cats; therefore all pets are mammals.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The subject term is universal in the conclusion but only partial in its premise.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is valid when a premise establishes the conclusion's full claim about the subject class.

fallacies.name: Illicit substitution of identicals
fallacies.summary: Replacing one expression with another that names the same thing in contexts where the substitution changes truth.
fallacies.body: Two names may refer to the same object while conveying different information to a person. In belief, quotation, and other intensional contexts, what someone knows or says may not survive substitution.

examples.text: Maya knows that the morning star is visible, so Maya knows that the evening star is visible, though she does not know they are the same object.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reasoning assumes co-reference guarantees interchangeable meaning in a belief or report context.
doesNotCountWhen: Substitution is valid in ordinary extensional claims when the names refer to the same object and context does not depend on the wording.

fallacies.name: Incomplete comparison
fallacies.summary: Claiming that one option is better, safer, or faster without stating the comparison point or measure.
fallacies.body: Comparative words require a baseline and dimension. Without them, the audience cannot tell what was compared or whether the advantage matters.

examples.text: The product is “safer” without saying safer than which product, under what conditions, or by what measure.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A comparative claim omits its relevant comparator or measurement basis.
doesNotCountWhen: A comparison is clear when the baseline and relevant metric are obvious from the stated context.

fallacies.name: Inconsistency
fallacies.summary: Maintaining claims or standards that conflict without acknowledging or resolving the conflict.
fallacies.body: People can revise views, distinguish contexts, or hold apparent tensions for a reason. The problem is using incompatible claims together as if both support the argument, with no account of the difference.

examples.text: A manager says every decision must follow the written policy, then rejects the policy whenever it constrains her own decisions.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The same speaker relies on incompatible propositions or standards in the same relevant context.
doesNotCountWhen: A change of view is not inconsistency when the change is acknowledged and reasons explain it.

fallacies.name: Inflation of conflict
fallacies.summary: Portraying a disagreement as deeper or more widespread than the actual points of dispute.
fallacies.body: People may share many premises while disagreeing about a narrow inference or value trade-off. Exaggerating the divide obscures common ground and can make resolution seem impossible.

examples.text: Two researchers disagree about one estimate, and a report says they reject each other's entire field.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A limited disagreement is represented as a total opposition without evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A dispute can be described as fundamental when the parties' actual commitments conflict at that level.

fallacies.name: Insignificant cause
fallacies.summary: Treating a minor factor as the main cause of a large outcome without showing that its effect is substantial.
fallacies.body: A small cause can matter in some systems, but magnitude and mechanism must be demonstrated. The argument overstates a weak contributor while ignoring larger causes.

examples.text: A tiny change in office lighting is blamed for the company's major revenue collapse, with no supporting link.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The proposed cause is too weak or disconnected to account for the scale of the effect claimed.
doesNotCountWhen: A small trigger can produce a large effect in a sensitive system when that mechanism is evidenced.

fallacies.name: Inverse-probability fallacy
fallacies.summary: Confusing the probability of evidence given a hypothesis with the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence.
fallacies.body: P(evidence|hypothesis) and P(hypothesis|evidence) answer different questions. A rare event can be likely to produce a clue while the clue still leaves the event unlikely overall, depending on base rates.

examples.text: A test is positive in 99% of cases with a condition, so a positive result is said to mean a 99% chance of the condition, ignoring false positives and prevalence.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conditional probability is reversed without incorporating prior rates and alternative explanations.
doesNotCountWhen: The reverse probability can be calculated when base rates and relevant likelihoods are included.

fallacies.name: Irrelevant reason
fallacies.summary: Offering a consideration that does not bear on the conclusion it is meant to support.
fallacies.body: The reason may be true and important in another context, but it has no demonstrated connection to the target claim. The argument needs to show why this fact changes the assessment.

examples.text: The new clinic must be safe because its waiting room is attractive.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The premise has no relevant inferential link to the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A fact becomes relevant when a supported causal, evidential, or normative connection to the conclusion is provided.

fallacies.name: Is–ought fallacy
fallacies.summary: Deriving a moral or prescriptive conclusion from facts alone without supplying a value premise.
fallacies.body: Descriptions of what happens do not by themselves say what should happen. The missing premise must explain why the observed fact creates a duty, permission, or goal.

examples.text: People often evade this tax, so the tax should be abolished.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A normative conclusion is inferred from descriptive premises with no bridge principle or value judgment.
doesNotCountWhen: An ought conclusion can follow when an explicit normative premise connects the facts to a duty or policy.

fallacies.name: Jumping to conclusions
fallacies.summary: Reaching a firm judgment before gathering enough relevant information or considering reasonable alternatives.
fallacies.body: The conclusion may eventually prove right, but it is premature relative to the available evidence. The error lies in confidence or timing, not merely in being wrong.

examples.text: A technician sees one warning light and declares the engine irreparable before running the diagnostic check.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A decisive conclusion is drawn from limited evidence while important checks or alternatives remain open.
doesNotCountWhen: A quick conclusion can be warranted when the evidence is decisive and further inquiry would not change the decision.

fallacies.name: Just-because fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating the bare fact that something happened or is asserted as an adequate explanation or reason.
fallacies.body: “Because” should connect an event to a cause or a conclusion to support. Repeating the event or asserting it happened does not supply that connection.

examples.text: The project failed because it failed; no cause or mechanism is identified.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The answer merely restates the claim or gives an unsupported assertion where an explanation is required.
doesNotCountWhen: A concise causal statement is sufficient when it names a supported cause, even without extended detail.

fallacies.name: Just-in-case fallacy
fallacies.summary: Using a remote possibility as enough reason for a costly precaution without weighing likelihood, harm, and trade-offs.
fallacies.body: Precaution can be sensible under uncertainty, especially for severe harm. The error is treating any imaginable risk as decisive, regardless of probability, cost, or whether the measure reduces it.

examples.text: Every building must install an expensive flood barrier because a flood is imaginable, though the site has no flood risk and the barrier creates hazards.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A merely conceivable danger is treated as decisive without proportional risk assessment.
doesNotCountWhen: Precaution is justified when the expected harm and uncertainty warrant the measure relative to its cost and side effects.

fallacies.name: Kettle logic
fallacies.summary: Defending a position with several incompatible excuses at once.
fallacies.body: The explanations cannot all be true together, or each shifts whenever challenged. This resembles the story of a kettle defended as never borrowed, returned undamaged, and already broken; inconsistency undermines the defense.

examples.text: The contractor says the work was completed, the deadline was impossible, and any delay was caused by the client.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Multiple defenses contradict one another or change opportunistically rather than jointly explaining the facts.
doesNotCountWhen: Several explanations can coexist when they address distinct events or are explicitly presented as alternatives.

fallacies.name: Least-plausible hypothesis
fallacies.summary: Selecting the least plausible explanation despite stronger ordinary alternatives, without evidence that favors it.
fallacies.body: An unusual account may be true, but it bears a higher explanatory burden when it requires unsupported assumptions. The reasoning fails by overlooking better-supported alternatives.

examples.text: A missing file is blamed on a sophisticated cyberattack before checking the recycle bin or access logs.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The preferred explanation is substantially less plausible and no evidence is offered to distinguish it from simpler candidates.
doesNotCountWhen: An extraordinary hypothesis is warranted when evidence uniquely or strongly favors it over ordinary explanations.

fallacies.name: Logic chopping
fallacies.summary: Using overly narrow technical distinctions to evade the practical substance of an objection.
fallacies.body: Precise distinctions are valuable when they affect the conclusion. They become evasive when the speaker subdivides language so finely that a valid criticism is dismissed while its underlying point remains unanswered.

examples.text: A firm says it did not “sell” customer data because it licensed access to the same data for payment.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A technical distinction is invoked without showing how it changes the relevant ethical, legal, or factual issue.
doesNotCountWhen: A precise distinction is legitimate when the difference is material under the rule being applied.

fallacies.name: Ludic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming real-world uncertainty can be represented by a neat, known set of probabilities like a simple game.
fallacies.body: In a game, possible outcomes and odds are specified; in real settings, the model may omit unknown events or changing processes. Treating model risk as fully measurable creates false confidence.

examples.text: A company estimates a one-in-a-million failure rate from a model and assumes no unmodeled failure mode is possible.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A neat probability model is treated as complete despite unknown outcomes, assumptions, or changing conditions.
doesNotCountWhen: A model is useful when assumptions and unmodeled uncertainty are disclosed and the decision is robust to them.

fallacies.name: Lump-of-labour fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming there is a fixed total amount of work, so one worker's job necessarily takes another's.
fallacies.body: Demand, productivity, and new tasks can change the amount and kind of work available. A specific job displacement can be real, but it does not prove total employment is a fixed pool.

examples.text: Automation removes some tasks, so it must permanently reduce the number of jobs by exactly the number of tasks automated.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Employment is treated as a fixed quantity without considering changing demand, productivity, or new work.
doesNotCountWhen: A fixed number of positions may exist in a particular budget or short-term setting; the claim must stay limited to that constraint.

fallacies.name: Magical thinking as causal inference
fallacies.summary: Treating a ritual, thought, or symbolic act as a cause of an event without evidence for a causal mechanism.
fallacies.body: A sequence or emotional association does not establish that the ritual affected the outcome. The claim needs controlled evidence that distinguishes causal influence from coincidence and ordinary mechanisms.

examples.text: The team wore lucky socks during a win, so the socks caused the victory.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A symbolic act is assigned causal power based on association or sequence alone.
doesNotCountWhen: A ritual can affect outcomes through known mechanisms such as confidence or coordination when those effects are evidenced.

fallacies.name: McNamara fallacy
fallacies.summary: Making a decision only from what can be measured while ignoring important factors that are difficult to quantify.
fallacies.body: Metrics support comparison, but a measure is a proxy for the goal, not the goal itself. Optimizing only measurable indicators can distort outcomes and exclude judgment about unmeasured costs or benefits.

examples.text: A school cuts art and counseling because test scores are the only outcomes in its dashboard.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The decision treats available metrics as the complete set of relevant values.
doesNotCountWhen: Quantitative measures are useful when they are valid for the goal and combined with relevant qualitative evidence.

fallacies.name: Middle-ground fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming the truth or fairest answer must lie halfway between two opposing claims.
fallacies.body: Compromise can be practical, but midpoint is not an evidential method. One side may be better supported, and the midpoint may be false or harmful.

examples.text: One engineer estimates a safe load at 10 tons and another at 30; the committee chooses 20 solely as the average.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A midpoint is treated as correct merely because it sits between competing positions.
doesNotCountWhen: A midpoint is justified when the measurement or negotiation gives a reason to average, not simply because views differ.

fallacies.name: Misleading vividness
fallacies.summary: Letting a vivid example dominate judgment while ignoring how representative or frequent it is.
fallacies.body: Concrete stories are memorable, which can make rare outcomes feel common. They can establish that something happened, but frequency and risk need broader data.

examples.text: One dramatic burglary leads a neighborhood to believe burglaries are increasing despite stable records.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A striking case is given more weight than representative evidence about the general pattern.
doesNotCountWhen: A vivid case is relevant to illustrate a possible harm or reveal a failure mode, but not by itself to estimate its rate.

fallacies.name: Missing-data fallacy
fallacies.summary: Drawing a conclusion from an incomplete dataset without accounting for the absent observations.
fallacies.body: Missingness may be random or may systematically remove the very cases that matter. Analysis that ignores why data are absent can bias the result.

examples.text: A survey of satisfied customers excludes people who stopped responding after a bad experience, then reports universal satisfaction.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The conclusion treats incomplete observations as representative without assessing the pattern or impact of missing data.
doesNotCountWhen: A conclusion can be sound when missing data are negligible or appropriately modeled and uncertainty is disclosed.

fallacies.name: Modal scope fallacy
fallacies.summary: Misplacing words such as “necessarily” or “possibly,” changing whether a claim or its subject is said to be necessary.
fallacies.body: “Necessarily, everyone is mortal” differs from “everyone is necessarily mortal.” The first says all people happen to be mortal; the second says each person could not have been otherwise. Scope changes the logical claim.

examples.text: It is necessary that every ticket holder has a seat, so every ticket holder necessarily has this seat.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument shifts the scope of a modal operator across a quantifier or proposition.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is valid when the modal term keeps the same scope or the relevant modal logic supports the move.

fallacies.name: Moralistic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Inferring that a factual description must be false because accepting it would be morally undesirable.
fallacies.body: Moral concerns can guide action but do not determine what is empirically true. Denying evidence because it seems to imply an unwelcome consequence reverses the relationship between values and facts.

examples.text: That difference between outcomes would be unfair, so the measured difference cannot be real.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A factual claim is rejected because its implications are judged morally bad, rather than because its evidence is weak.
doesNotCountWhen: Ethical considerations can affect what should be done with a fact, not whether the measurement occurred.

fallacies.name: Motte-and-bailey
fallacies.summary: Alternating between a bold, controversial claim and a modest, defensible one as if they were the same position.
fallacies.body: The speaker advances the bold claim when persuading, then retreats to the modest claim when challenged and accuses critics of attacking the safer version. The two propositions need to be kept distinct.

examples.text: A commentator claims that all regulation destroys freedom, then says the claim only means some rules can be burdensome.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The speaker retreats from a strong thesis to a weaker one without acknowledging the change, then treats defense of the weaker thesis as support for the stronger.
doesNotCountWhen: Refining a claim is legitimate when the revision is explicit and the original is no longer presented as established.

fallacies.name: Moving the goalposts
fallacies.summary: Changing the standard for accepting evidence after the other side has met the original standard.
fallacies.body: If criteria shift only when satisfied, the claim becomes impossible to test and no evidence can count. A revised standard can be reasonable if new information reveals a genuine flaw and the revision is applied consistently.

examples.text: After a trial meets the agreed success threshold, the critic demands a larger trial without explaining why the first threshold was inadequate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The acceptance condition changes in response to success, without an independent reason for the new requirement.
doesNotCountWhen: Updating criteria for a documented methodological reason is sound when the change is transparent and not selectively applied.

fallacies.name: Multiple-comparisons fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating a striking result among many statistical tests as meaningful without accounting for the chance of a false positive.
fallacies.body: When enough comparisons are tried, some will look significant by chance. Selecting the best-looking result without correction or disclosure exaggerates evidence.

examples.text: A study tests 100 outcomes and reports the one with p<.05 as proof, ignoring the other 99 tests.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Many hypotheses were examined, but the selected result is interpreted as if it were the only planned test.
doesNotCountWhen: A result can remain persuasive when tests were pre-registered, multiplicity is controlled, or independent replication confirms it.

fallacies.name: Name-calling as refutation
fallacies.summary: Using a derogatory label as though it disproved the proposition being discussed.
fallacies.body: A label can describe conduct when properly supported, but it does not replace an argument about truth. The audience is pushed to reject the claim through stigma rather than evidence.

examples.text: That proposal is communist, so its cost estimate is wrong.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A name or category label is presented as a reason the claim is false.
doesNotCountWhen: A label may be relevant when a precise definition and evidence show the classification itself bears on the issue.

fallacies.name: Naturalistic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating a natural property or description as a complete definition of moral goodness.
fallacies.body: In its philosophical sense, the error attempts to reduce “good” to a natural feature such as pleasure or evolutionary fitness, as though that identity needed no argument. It is distinct from the broader appeal-to-nature claim that natural things are better.

examples.text: Good simply means biologically advantageous; therefore any trait that aids reproduction is morally good.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A moral term is defined as a natural property and the definition is treated as settling the evaluative question.
doesNotCountWhen: A moral theory may argue that a natural property grounds value, but it must defend that account rather than assume identity by definition.

fallacies.name: Negating antecedent and consequent
fallacies.summary: Treating a conditional's two parts as though denying one automatically denies the other, or reverses their relation.
fallacies.body: A one-way conditional does not establish equivalence. From if A then B, not-A does not imply not-B, and B does not imply A; both moves require stronger premises.

examples.text: If the alarm is armed, the light flashes; the alarm is not armed, so the light cannot flash.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reasoning infers a negated consequent from a negated antecedent or otherwise treats a one-way conditional as biconditional.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference is sound when the conditional is explicitly biconditional or alternatives are excluded.

fallacies.name: Negative conclusion from affirmative premises
fallacies.summary: In categorical logic, drawing a negative conclusion from two affirmative premises.
fallacies.body: Affirmative premises connect categories but do not establish that any two categories are separate. A negative conclusion needs a negative premise to support exclusion.

examples.text: All nurses are trained; some volunteers are nurses; therefore some volunteers are not trained.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Both categorical premises are affirmative, yet the conclusion asserts exclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A negative conclusion can follow when a premise explicitly establishes the relevant separation.

fallacies.name: Nirvana fallacy
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a workable option because it does not achieve a perfect or risk-free ideal.
fallacies.body: Real choices often involve trade-offs. Comparing an imperfect proposal with an unattainable perfect alternative makes every practical improvement look inadequate.

examples.text: The new filter removes 95% of contaminants, so it is useless because it does not remove 100%.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A feasible option is dismissed solely for failing an idealized standard while its real-world alternatives are ignored.
doesNotCountWhen: A high threshold is justified when the remaining risk is unacceptable and a feasible safer option exists.

fallacies.name: No true Scotsman
fallacies.summary: Protecting a broad generalization by redefining the group so counterexamples no longer count.
fallacies.body: Instead of revising the claim, the speaker adds an unsupported purity condition. This makes the generalization immune to evidence by excluding inconvenient cases after the fact.

examples.text: No local shop sells expired food. When one does, the speaker says it was not a “true” local shop.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A counterexample is excluded by an ad hoc definition not part of the original claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Clarifying a group's established definition is legitimate when the criterion existed before the counterexample and is applied consistently.

fallacies.name: Non sequitur
fallacies.summary: Drawing a conclusion that does not logically or evidentially follow from the stated premises.
fallacies.body: The premises may be true, but a missing connection leaves the conclusion unsupported. Naming the gap—causal, categorical, or relevance-based—helps show what additional premise would be needed.

examples.text: The building has blue doors, so its heating system is efficient.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: No supported inferential link connects the reasons to the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: The inference becomes valid when a relevant linking premise or evidence is supplied.

fallacies.name: Non-recognition fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating failure to recognize or notice something as proof that it does not exist or matter.
fallacies.body: Observation depends on attention, access, and detection. A person may miss a real pattern, so nonrecognition alone cannot establish absence.

examples.text: I do not see any discrimination in the hiring process, so none occurs.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Personal or institutional failure to notice is used as evidence that the phenomenon is absent.
doesNotCountWhen: A reliable, comprehensive search that would detect the phenomenon can make non-detection informative.

fallacies.name: Notable-effort fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating effort, sacrifice, or hard work as proof that a result is correct or successful.
fallacies.body: Effort may deserve recognition, but the quality of an outcome depends on whether the method worked. Sunk labor does not validate a conclusion or remedy.

examples.text: The team spent two years on the forecast, so it must be accurate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Investment of effort is offered as the warrant for correctness or effectiveness.
doesNotCountWhen: Effort can be relevant to assessing diligence or commitment, while the result still needs independent evidence.

fallacies.name: Nutpicking
fallacies.summary: Selecting an extreme or eccentric member of a group and presenting that person as representative of the whole.
fallacies.body: A fringe statement can be genuinely held without defining a movement or position. The argument uses the most embarrassing example to avoid the strongest, ordinary version of the view.

examples.text: One obscure activist makes an extreme demand, and the speaker claims it represents everyone who supports reform.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An outlier is used as the face of a broader group without evidence of representativeness.
doesNotCountWhen: An individual's statement can establish that at least one person holds it; claims about prevalence need broader evidence.

fallacies.name: Obscurum per obscurius
fallacies.summary: Explaining an unclear thing with an even more obscure or unexplained concept.
fallacies.body: An explanation should reduce uncertainty. Replacing one unknown with a less familiar unknown leaves the original question unresolved and may only make the account sound sophisticated.

examples.text: The machine fails because of “ontological flux,” a term that is not defined or operationalized.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The proposed cause is less clear or less testable than the phenomenon it claims to explain.
doesNotCountWhen: A technical concept is explanatory when it is defined and independently connected to observable consequences.

fallacies.name: Overexplanation
fallacies.summary: Adding excessive, irrelevant detail that obscures the point or creates a misleading impression of support.
fallacies.body: More words do not equal more evidence. Detail can bury a missing inference, distract from a direct question, or make a weak account seem comprehensive.

examples.text: Asked whether the funds were transferred, an official gives a long history of the department but never states whether the transfer occurred.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The volume or tangential detail prevents the central claim or answer from being assessed.
doesNotCountWhen: A detailed account is useful when the information is relevant and clarifies the reasoning or evidence.

fallacies.name: Overextended analogy
fallacies.summary: Pushing a useful comparison beyond the respects in which the cases are alike.
fallacies.body: An analogy can illuminate one feature but cannot carry every property of one case into another. The inference goes wrong when additional conclusions rely on similarities that were never established.

examples.text: Because a school is like a family in some ways, the principal claims parental authority over students' private lives.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A comparison that supports one limited point is stretched to justify further claims without relevant similarity.
doesNotCountWhen: An analogy remains sound when conclusions stay within the specific shared features it establishes.

fallacies.name: Overextended outrage
fallacies.summary: Escalating a justified criticism into condemnation far beyond what the evidence supports.
fallacies.body: Moral concern can be warranted while the scale of blame or consequence is not. Exaggerated language may distract from the actual conduct and make proportional judgment harder.

examples.text: A clerical mistake is called proof that the entire organization is criminal.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The intensity or breadth of condemnation exceeds the established action and its consequences.
doesNotCountWhen: Strong condemnation is justified when evidence establishes serious, widespread, or intentional harm.

fallacies.name: Overgeneralization
fallacies.summary: Extending a pattern beyond the cases, time, or conditions for which evidence supports it.
fallacies.body: The conclusion may begin with a real observation but ignores limits and variation. It turns “often” or “in this setting” into “always” or “everywhere.”

examples.text: This medication helped some trial participants, so it will help every patient with any related condition.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A limited finding is stated as a universal or context-free rule.
doesNotCountWhen: A broad generalization is warranted when representative evidence covers the stated population and conditions.

fallacies.name: Overwhelming exception
fallacies.summary: Using a small number of exceptions to obscure a strong general pattern, or using one exception to invalidate the rule entirely.
fallacies.body: Exceptions can limit a general claim but need to be weighed in proportion. The argument misleads when rare cases are made to dominate a pattern, or when a single counterexample is treated as erasing every useful regularity.

examples.text: Most flights arrive on time, but one delay is used to claim airlines never keep schedules.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The exception's significance is overstated relative to the frequency and scope of the general pattern.
doesNotCountWhen: A counterexample defeats a truly universal claim; it does not by itself erase a probabilistic trend.

fallacies.name: Package-deal fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating several distinct ideas or policies as an inseparable bundle so agreement with one is taken to require all.
fallacies.body: The bundle may hide disagreement about individual parts. Each component needs its own justification unless a real dependency shows they must be adopted together.

examples.text: To support public transit, a speaker says voters must also endorse every part of the unrelated city platform.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Separate propositions are bundled and one is used to pressure acceptance of the others.
doesNotCountWhen: A package is justified when its components are genuinely interdependent and the reasons for that dependency are shown.

fallacies.name: Pathetic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Attributing human emotions or intentions to nature and treating that personification as an explanation.
fallacies.body: Weather or landscape can be described poetically, but nature does not literally express human feelings. The metaphor becomes faulty reasoning when a supposed emotion is used to explain an event or prescribe a response.

examples.text: The storm is angry with us, so the town must cancel the project to appease it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Human feeling attributed to nature is treated as a literal cause or reason.
doesNotCountWhen: Personification is harmless literary language when no factual inference depends on it.

fallacies.name: Persuasive definition
fallacies.summary: Defining a term in an emotionally favorable or unfavorable way to influence judgment while appearing merely to explain it.
fallacies.body: The definition quietly attaches approval or blame to the label. The audience may accept the value judgment because it is embedded in vocabulary rather than argued for.

examples.text: A “responsible citizen” is defined as someone who supports the speaker's policy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A definition carries a contested evaluation that then does argumentative work.
doesNotCountWhen: A clear stipulative definition is acceptable when its evaluative purpose is explicit and not mistaken for evidence.

fallacies.name: Poisoning the well
fallacies.summary: Preemptively discrediting a person so an audience will reject anything they later say.
fallacies.body: The attack comes before the claim and frames it as untrustworthy in advance. A source's record can be relevant, but broad stigmatization does not answer future evidence.

examples.text: Before the auditor presents findings, the director calls her a disgruntled troublemaker whose report should be ignored.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A speaker is discredited in advance to bias reception of their argument rather than address its content.
doesNotCountWhen: A specific, evidenced conflict may be disclosed before testimony so the audience can weigh it, while still examining the claim.

fallacies.name: Political-correctness fallacy
fallacies.summary: Dismissing a claim as mere “political correctness” instead of addressing its evidence or reasoning.
fallacies.body: The label implies that a position is motivated by social pressure rather than truth, but that attribution does not show the position is false. It functions as a shortcut around the argument.

examples.text: The safety concern is just political correctness, so the complaint about the hazard can be ignored.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The pejorative label substitutes for an answer to the stated reasons.
doesNotCountWhen: Social incentives may be relevant context when evidenced, but the claim still stands or falls on its support.

fallacies.name: Possibility-to-certainty fallacy
fallacies.summary: Moving from “this could happen” to “this will happen” without evidence that raises possibility to certainty.
fallacies.body: Possibility only excludes impossibility; it does not establish likelihood or inevitability. The argument inflates a scenario into a prediction.

examples.text: The proposed software could fail, so it will definitely fail during launch.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A possible outcome is asserted as certain without added evidence or a necessary causal link.
doesNotCountWhen: Certainty follows when the outcome is logically entailed or evidence makes alternatives impossible.

fallacies.name: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
fallacies.summary: Assuming that an earlier event caused a later one merely because it came first.
fallacies.body: Temporal order is necessary for many causes but not sufficient to prove causation. Other causes, coincidence, and reverse or indirect relationships need consideration.

examples.text: A town changed its logo, then tourism rose, so the logo caused the increase despite a new airport opening at the same time.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument infers cause from sequence alone without ruling out alternatives or establishing mechanism.
doesNotCountWhen: A before-and-after comparison supports causation when other changes and baseline trends are addressed.

fallacies.name: Pragmatic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating a claim as true because believing or acting on it would be useful or convenient.
fallacies.body: Practical consequences can guide decisions, but they do not determine a proposition's truth. A useful belief may be false, and an inconvenient fact may still be true.

examples.text: It would help morale if the test results were positive, so the results should be reported as positive.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Practical usefulness is offered as evidence that a factual claim is true.
doesNotCountWhen: Pragmatic considerations are relevant to choosing an action under uncertainty, with the factual uncertainty kept explicit.

fallacies.name: Prejudicial language
fallacies.summary: Using loaded wording to shape judgment before the evidence has been considered.
fallacies.body: A label can frame the same act as heroic or shameful without establishing which description is accurate. The argument relies on connotation instead of showing the relevant facts and standards.

examples.text: The proposal is called a “handout” before any account of who qualifies or what it funds.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Emotionally loaded language carries the conclusion without supplying support.
doesNotCountWhen: Evaluative terms are appropriate when their criteria are stated and the evidence meets them.

fallacies.name: Presuming truth from lack of disproof
fallacies.summary: Treating a claim as true because nobody has disproved it.
fallacies.body: The absence of refutation does not shift the claim's evidential burden automatically. Some claims are difficult to test, and lack of contrary evidence may reflect limited inquiry.

examples.text: No one has disproved that the vault contains a hidden room, so the room exists.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The claimant presents failure to disprove as sufficient proof, without showing a strong test should have found disconfirmation.
doesNotCountWhen: A well-tested claim can gain support when repeated attempts to falsify it fail, but only if those tests were capable of detecting error.

fallacies.name: Proof by intimidation
fallacies.summary: Using ridicule, threats, or status pressure to discourage scrutiny and make a claim seem established.
fallacies.body: Intimidation changes the social cost of disagreement, not the evidential status of the proposition. The audience may comply without being persuaded by reasons.

examples.text: The supervisor says only an incompetent person would question the calculation, then refuses to show the work.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Pressure or humiliation is used to suppress challenge in place of an argument.
doesNotCountWhen: Firmly challenging a claim is not intimidation when criticism is directed at its reasons and allows a response.

fallacies.name: Proof surrogate
fallacies.summary: Offering a proxy for proof, such as confidence or technical display, in place of evidence that actually bears on the claim.
fallacies.body: A surrogate resembles the outward signs of expertise or demonstration but does not establish the proposition. The audience is asked to mistake performance for a valid evidential connection.

examples.text: A chart with many decimals is shown as proof that a policy works, though it contains no comparison group or outcome measure.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A display, credential, or ritual of proof is substituted for relevant evidence or valid inference.
doesNotCountWhen: A proxy measure can support a conclusion when its relationship to the target claim is validated and explained.

fallacies.name: Prosecutor's fallacy
fallacies.summary: Confusing the probability of evidence under innocence with the probability of innocence given the evidence.
fallacies.body: A rare match can be unlikely if a person is innocent, yet it does not by itself show the chance that the person is innocent. That reverse probability also depends on how many possible suspects there are and other evidence.
