examples.text: A DNA profile is a one-in-a-million match, so there is only a one-in-a-million chance the accused is innocent.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The likelihood of the evidence under one hypothesis is presented as the posterior probability of that hypothesis without base rates.
doesNotCountWhen: A posterior estimate is sound when it incorporates prior odds, the match likelihood, and relevant alternative sources.

fallacies.name: Psychogenetic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a belief because of a supposed psychological origin rather than assessing its truth.
fallacies.body: Explaining why someone came to believe a proposition does not determine whether it is true. The argument uses a diagnosis, trauma, or desire as a substitute for evidence.

examples.text: He believes the policy is unsafe only because he is anxious, so the policy is safe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A psychological account of the belief is treated as a refutation of the believed proposition.
doesNotCountWhen: Psychological factors may help assess testimony or decision-making, but independent evidence remains necessary to settle the claim.

fallacies.name: Quantifier-shift fallacy
fallacies.summary: Changing the scope of words such as “all,” “some,” or “each” so a conclusion says more than the premise.
fallacies.body: “Everyone loves someone” does not mean there is one person whom everyone loves. The order and scope of quantifiers determine whether the claim is about different individuals or a single shared one.

examples.text: Every student read a book, so there is one book that every student read.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument swaps quantifier order or scope without a premise that supports the stronger reading.
doesNotCountWhen: The conclusion follows when the quantified individuals and objects are explicitly the same or the premise states the stronger scope.

fallacies.name: Quantum-physics fallacy
fallacies.summary: Invoking quantum physics as a vague explanation or license for claims that do not follow from the relevant theory.
fallacies.body: Quantum mechanics has precise mathematical content; its counterintuitive results do not support arbitrary claims about consciousness, healing, or everyday causation. The speaker must identify a specific result and show how it applies.

examples.text: A treatment works because quantum energy lets thoughts directly rearrange cells, with no defined mechanism or evidence.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Quantum terminology is used as authority while the claimed application is unspecified or unsupported.
doesNotCountWhen: A quantum explanation is appropriate when the system, model, and empirical connection are genuinely relevant.

fallacies.name: Questionable premise
fallacies.summary: Building an argument on a premise that is uncertain, unsupported, or more contested than the conclusion.
fallacies.body: Even valid reasoning cannot establish a conclusion if its key starting point lacks support. The premise must be defended rather than smuggled in as settled.

examples.text: Since the new rule has already reduced crime, the city should expand it, though no crime data are offered.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument depends materially on a premise whose truth has not been established.
doesNotCountWhen: A premise need not be re-proven in every exchange when it is well-supported or legitimately shared background.

fallacies.name: Quoting out of context
fallacies.summary: Using a quotation after removing surrounding material that changes its meaning or qualification.
fallacies.body: The words may be accurately copied yet misrepresent the speaker's position because context supplies scope, irony, or a condition. The quotation must be checked against the full passage and purpose.

examples.text: A report quotes “the plan could fail” but omits the next sentence, “only if the backup system also fails,” to portray the speaker as predicting failure.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The omitted context materially changes the quoted claim's meaning or force.
doesNotCountWhen: A short quotation is fair when the omitted text does not alter the relevant meaning and the source is represented accurately.

fallacies.name: Red herring
fallacies.summary: Introducing an irrelevant distraction that shifts attention away from the issue under discussion.
fallacies.body: A red herring can be related in theme yet fail to answer the central question. Its function is to redirect attention, not establish the disputed conclusion.

examples.text: Asked whether expenses exceeded the limit, the director discusses how hard the team worked.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response changes the subject and leaves the original issue unresolved.
doesNotCountWhen: A new point is not a distraction when it directly affects the decision or answers the question.

fallacies.name: Reductio ad Hitlerum
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a proposal by associating it with Hitler or Nazis rather than assessing its actual merits.
fallacies.body: An idea's adoption by a notorious person does not make every version of it wrong. Historical association matters only if the relevant features and consequences are shared and argued.

examples.text: A public health measure was used in Nazi Germany, so any modern version is evil.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The Nazi association is treated as sufficient refutation without showing a relevant connection.
doesNotCountWhen: Historical comparison is valid when specific shared policies, mechanisms, or harms are established rather than invoked as a label.

fallacies.name: Regression fallacy
fallacies.summary: Mistaking a return toward the average after an unusually high or low result for an effect of an intervention.
fallacies.body: Extreme outcomes are often followed by less extreme ones even without treatment. If action is taken at the peak or trough, the natural regression can be wrongly credited to it.

examples.text: A player has an unusually poor game, receives coaching, then performs normally; the coach is credited without considering regression to the mean.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Improvement or decline after an extreme result is attributed to an intervention without comparison or baseline trend.
doesNotCountWhen: An intervention's effect is supported when it exceeds the expected return to average, measured against suitable controls.

fallacies.name: Reification
fallacies.summary: Treating an abstract idea or statistical construct as though it were a concrete agent or object.
fallacies.body: Abstractions can summarize real patterns, but they do not act independently of people and mechanisms. Reification hides the actual causes by giving an abstract label agency.

examples.text: The market punished the workers, so no policy decision needs to be examined.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An abstract concept is treated as a literal causal actor rather than shorthand for underlying processes.
doesNotCountWhen: Personifying an abstraction is harmless shorthand when the actual mechanisms remain clear.

fallacies.name: Relative privation
fallacies.summary: Dismissing a real problem because another problem is worse.
fallacies.body: Comparative severity does not make a lesser harm nonexistent or irrelevant. Resources may require prioritization, but that requires comparing costs and consequences rather than using worse suffering to silence discussion.

examples.text: The leaking school roof should not be fixed because another district has no school at all.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A problem is dismissed solely by pointing to a more serious one, with no allocation analysis.
doesNotCountWhen: Prioritizing a more urgent need is reasonable when the limited resource and comparative consequences are addressed.

fallacies.name: Reverse causation
fallacies.summary: Assuming the direction of cause is opposite from what the evidence supports, or confusing which variable influences which.
fallacies.body: An observed relationship alone may not establish direction. The outcome might cause the supposed cause, or both may be driven by something else.

examples.text: People with more health visits have worse health, so visits cause illness, though illness leads to visits.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument assigns a causal direction without evidence about timing or mechanism and ignores reverse influence.
doesNotCountWhen: A directional claim is supported when the order and mechanism are established and alternatives are tested.

fallacies.name: Righteousness fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating the moral rightness of a cause as proof that a particular claim or tactic is correct.
fallacies.body: A worthy goal does not guarantee that every supporting statement is true or every method justified. The argument transfers moral approval of the end to disputed means or facts.

examples.text: The campaign seeks justice, so its unverified accusation must be accurate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Moral alignment with a cause is used as proof of a factual claim or specific tactic.
doesNotCountWhen: A moral principle can justify action when the relevant facts and connection to the action are established.

fallacies.name: Rights-to-ought fallacy
fallacies.summary: Inferring that someone ought to exercise a right merely because they are entitled to do so.
fallacies.body: Having permission or a right does not create a duty to use it. The argument confuses what is allowed with what is advisable, required, or morally best.

examples.text: Workers have a right to strike, so they must strike now.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An entitlement is treated as a requirement or recommendation without a further value premise.
doesNotCountWhen: A right can support a choice, while separate reasons explain whether exercising it is prudent or obligatory.

fallacies.name: Scapegoating
fallacies.summary: Blaming a person or group for a complex problem without sufficient evidence that they caused it.
fallacies.body: Scapegoating offers a simple target for diffuse failures and can redirect attention from broader causes or responsible decision-makers. A causal claim needs evidence about actual contribution.

examples.text: The town's budget deficit is blamed on newcomers despite spending and revenue records showing no such effect.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A group is assigned responsibility for a problem beyond what evidence establishes, often to divert blame.
doesNotCountWhen: Holding an actor responsible is warranted when evidence shows their actions materially contributed to the outcome.

fallacies.name: Self-righteousness fallacy
fallacies.summary: Using one's own moral purity or certainty as proof that one's position is correct.
fallacies.body: A person's good intentions or sense of virtue do not validate their factual claims. Self-certainty can insulate a view from correction and shift debate from evidence to character.

examples.text: I care more about the community than anyone here, so my account of the budget is right.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Moral self-praise is offered as a warrant for a factual or policy conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A person's values can explain their priorities, but the conclusion still needs relevant reasons and evidence.

fallacies.name: Self-sealing argument
fallacies.summary: Defining every possible outcome as confirmation so no evidence could count against the claim.
fallacies.body: A useful hypothesis risks being wrong under some observable conditions. A self-sealing account reinterprets disconfirmation as further proof, making it impossible to distinguish from alternatives.

examples.text: The device works when it activates; when it does not, that proves it is silently transmitting energy.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The claim has no possible counterevidence because contrary outcomes are reclassified as support.
doesNotCountWhen: A theory can be difficult to test without being self-sealing if it still specifies outcomes that would count against it.

fallacies.name: Self-selection fallacy
fallacies.summary: Generalizing from people who chose to participate as if they represented everyone.
fallacies.body: Volunteers or respondents often differ from nonparticipants in motivation, experience, or outcome. Their answers may be accurate for them but biased as a population estimate.

examples.text: A poll of people who called a complaint hotline is used to estimate how satisfied all customers are.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Participation is self-selected and likely related to the measured outcome, but the result is generalized without adjustment.
doesNotCountWhen: Volunteer samples can answer questions about volunteers or be corrected when selection effects are understood.

fallacies.name: Shifting the burden of proof
fallacies.summary: Demanding that a critic disprove a claim instead of the claimant supporting it.
fallacies.body: The person asserting a proposition bears the initial burden to provide evidence. A critic's inability to disprove it does not establish it, though a critic may owe support for a counterclaim.

examples.text: The product is safe because regulators cannot prove that it is dangerous.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The claimant uses the opponent's failure to disprove as proof while offering no adequate support.
doesNotCountWhen: Burden can shift after a claim has met an appropriate evidential threshold or when the critic advances a new claim.

fallacies.name: Shoehorning
fallacies.summary: Forcing evidence or a case into a favored category even though important features do not fit.
fallacies.body: Classification helps reasoning only when criteria are applied consistently. Shoe-horning protects a theory by stretching definitions around inconvenient observations rather than revising the theory.

examples.text: A failed prediction is labeled a success by redefining “success” to include any result.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The category is broadened or distorted only to absorb an awkward case and preserve the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: A category can be revised when the reason is explicit and the new criteria apply consistently to all cases.

fallacies.name: Simpleton's fallacy
fallacies.summary: Rejecting a view by portraying its supporters as simple-minded, without addressing the view's reasons.
fallacies.body: The insult treats disagreement as evidence of ignorance and pressures the audience to conform. It does not establish that the proposition is false.

examples.text: Only simpletons believe the water test; therefore the test results can be ignored.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A person's intelligence or sophistication is attacked in place of the argument.
doesNotCountWhen: Explaining a specific knowledge gap is relevant when it bears on testimony, but labels do not refute the claim.

fallacies.name: Slippery-slope fallacy
fallacies.summary: Claiming that one step will trigger a chain of increasingly extreme outcomes without establishing the links.
fallacies.body: A chain can be real if each stage makes the next likely or unavoidable. The fallacy skips evidence for those transitions and treats a remote endpoint as inevitable.

examples.text: Allowing one late submission will end all deadlines and destroy the school, with no mechanism connecting the steps.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The predicted chain lacks evidence for one or more causal or policy transitions.
doesNotCountWhen: A slope argument is sound when each link is supported and the cumulative likelihood is responsibly assessed.

fallacies.name: Small-sample fallacy
fallacies.summary: Drawing a strong statistical conclusion from too few observations to distinguish a pattern from chance.
fallacies.body: Small samples have high uncertainty and may overrepresent unusual cases. The issue is not simply sample size but whether it can support the precision and scope claimed.

examples.text: Two customer complaints are used to conclude that most users hate the redesign.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The sample is too small for the claimed estimate or population generalization, given variability.
doesNotCountWhen: A small sample can support a narrow observation or a preliminary signal if uncertainty is made clear.

fallacies.name: Special pleading
fallacies.summary: Applying a standard to a case and then inventing an unsupported exception when the standard becomes inconvenient.
fallacies.body: Exceptions can be principled, but they need a relevant reason that applies consistently. Special pleading exempts the favored case without showing why it differs in a way that matters.

examples.text: The manager says every expense needs a receipt, except her own purchases because she is trusted.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: An exception is asserted without a relevant criterion or is applied only to protect the favored case.
doesNotCountWhen: A justified exception follows an explicit, relevant rule applied consistently.

fallacies.name: Spin doctoring
fallacies.summary: Presenting facts with selective framing to steer interpretation while obscuring material context.
fallacies.body: Spin may use technically true statements, but its framing emphasizes favorable details and minimizes unfavorable ones. The audience is led to a conclusion the complete record may not support.

examples.text: A report calls a 2% sales fall “nearly flat” while omitting the 30% rise in returns.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The presentation's selective emphasis materially distorts how the full evidence bears on the conclusion.
doesNotCountWhen: Concise framing is fair when material context is disclosed and the wording does not mislead about the overall record.

fallacies.name: Spiritual fallacy
fallacies.summary: Using a spiritual explanation or experience as decisive evidence for an unrelated factual claim.
fallacies.body: Spiritual beliefs can guide personal meaning and practice. The inferential gap appears when a subjective experience is treated as proof of an external, testable event without corroboration.

examples.text: I felt a healing presence, so the tumor has disappeared.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A spiritual interpretation is treated as conclusive evidence for a measurable external claim.
doesNotCountWhen: A spiritual account can support a claim within shared religious premises, while medical or other empirical outcomes require their own evidence.

fallacies.name: Spotlight fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming a visible or frequently reported example represents the overall pattern because attention is focused on it.
fallacies.body: What receives attention is not necessarily common. Media coverage, salience, and availability can make rare events seem typical unless frequency is checked against broader data.

examples.text: Several heavily reported shark attacks lead someone to claim attacks are increasing, without rate data.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A prominent case is mistaken for evidence of prevalence or trend.
doesNotCountWhen: A spotlighted example can illustrate a real risk; estimating frequency requires representative data.

fallacies.name: Stolen-concept fallacy
fallacies.summary: Using a concept while denying the more basic concepts that make it possible to use coherently.
fallacies.body: The claim depends on the very standard or distinction it rejects. Identifying the dependency shows an internal inconsistency, not merely disagreement about definitions.

examples.text: Someone argues that no statements can be true, while presenting that sentence as a true statement.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument's conclusion undermines a premise or conceptual tool required by the argument itself.
doesNotCountWhen: A position is not self-undermining when it rejects a concept in a limited domain while relying on it elsewhere consistently.

fallacies.name: Straw man
fallacies.summary: Replacing an opponent's actual argument with a distorted, weaker version and attacking that substitute.
fallacies.body: The rebuttal may defeat the substitute but leaves the real claim unanswered. A fair criticism should preserve the opponent's central point and important qualifications.

examples.text: A proposal to limit one pesticide is answered as if it demanded banning all farming chemicals.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response attacks a materially distorted restatement rather than the position actually defended.
doesNotCountWhen: A concise paraphrase is fair when the opponent would recognize it and it retains the relevant qualifications.

fallacies.name: Style over substance
fallacies.summary: Judging an argument by polished delivery or presentation while overlooking the quality of its reasons.
fallacies.body: Fluency, graphics, and confidence can make a message persuasive without making it sound. The claim's evidence and inference need evaluation independent of its style.

examples.text: A beautifully designed chart is accepted despite using a misleading scale and unsupported data.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Presentation quality substitutes for checking the factual basis or logic.
doesNotCountWhen: Clear style improves communication; it becomes evidence only when it helps expose sound reasoning, not in place of it.

fallacies.name: Subjectivist fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating a personal preference or feeling as if it settled an objective question for everyone.
fallacies.body: A person is authoritative about their own experience, but a preference does not establish external facts or universal standards. The argument moves from “I feel” to “it is” without a bridge.

examples.text: I dislike the taste, so the food is objectively unsafe.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A subjective reaction is used to prove a claim that exceeds the person's own experience.
doesNotCountWhen: Subjective reports are valid evidence about the reporter's experience or preference.

fallacies.name: Subverted support
fallacies.summary: Presenting apparent support that is undermined by a qualification, source, or condition the audience is not meant to notice.
fallacies.body: The argument appears to cite evidence, but the support does not actually back the conclusion once its limitations are included. This can happen through buried caveats or misrepresented data.

examples.text: A study is cited as proving the program works, while its results section says the measured effect was indistinguishable from zero.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The cited support is materially qualified or contradicted, and the presentation obscures that fact.
doesNotCountWhen: Qualified evidence can still support a limited conclusion when its uncertainty and scope are stated accurately.

fallacies.name: Sunk-cost fallacy
fallacies.summary: Continuing a failing course because of resources already spent, rather than comparing future costs and benefits.
fallacies.body: Past costs cannot be recovered and should not determine what is best from now on. The decision should compare expected future outcomes of continuing and stopping.

examples.text: The company keeps funding a failing product because it has already spent millions developing it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Irrecoverable past investment is treated as a reason to incur more costs.
doesNotCountWhen: Past investment can matter indirectly if it produced usable assets or obligations that change future options; sunk cost itself is not recoverable.

fallacies.name: Suppressed evidence
fallacies.summary: Leaving out relevant evidence that would materially weaken the conclusion.
fallacies.body: Unlike ordinary brevity, suppression creates a misleading impression by concealing counterevidence needed for an accurate assessment. The omitted evidence may alter the result or confidence.

examples.text: A safety summary reports successful tests but omits a serious failure under the exact operating condition at issue.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Relevant contrary evidence is withheld or ignored while a conclusion is presented as complete.
doesNotCountWhen: A concise argument may omit immaterial details; it should disclose evidence that changes the conclusion's strength or scope.

fallacies.name: Taboo argument
fallacies.summary: Treating a claim as unchallengeable because discussing it is prohibited or socially forbidden.
fallacies.body: A taboo may protect people from harm, but silence does not prove a claim true or false. The argument uses the prohibition itself to settle the dispute rather than evaluating the claim under appropriate standards.

examples.text: No one may question the leader's forecast, so the forecast must be correct.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The fact that a topic is forbidden is presented as evidence for a proposition about it.
doesNotCountWhen: Some topics require limits on harmful conduct or disclosure; those limits do not make factual claims automatically true.

fallacies.name: Texas-sharpshooter fallacy
fallacies.summary: Highlighting a pattern after the fact while ignoring how many other patterns could have been selected.
fallacies.body: If data are searched broadly, clusters will appear by chance. Choosing one cluster after seeing the results and then treating it as a predicted pattern overstates evidence.

examples.text: A company plots many product metrics, circles the one that improved, and claims its strategy predicted that success.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The pattern or metric was selected after inspecting many possibilities, without accounting for selection.
doesNotCountWhen: A pre-specified pattern replicated in new data is stronger evidence than a post hoc cluster.

fallacies.name: There-is-no-alternative fallacy
fallacies.summary: Claiming a proposal is unavoidable because no alternative exists, without adequately examining options.
fallacies.body: The phrase turns a preferred choice into necessity and can discourage search for compromises or different goals. Genuine constraints should be demonstrated, not asserted.

examples.text: The only way to fund the service is this fee increase, though other budget options were not considered.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument asserts the absence of alternatives without surveying plausible options or constraints.
doesNotCountWhen: A choice may be necessary when meaningful alternatives have been identified and ruled out for stated reasons.

fallacies.name: Tokenism
fallacies.summary: Using one or a few members of an underrepresented group as proof that a system is inclusive or unbiased.
fallacies.body: Presence of an individual does not show fair access, influence, or representative treatment. The example is made to carry a system-level conclusion it cannot establish.

examples.text: One woman is on the board, so the organization cannot have a gender barrier.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A token instance is used to dismiss evidence about broader representation or structural conditions.
doesNotCountWhen: A specific person's inclusion is evidence about that person's participation; broader claims require wider measures.

fallacies.name: Traitorous-critic fallacy
fallacies.summary: Dismissing criticism as betrayal or disloyalty instead of answering its substance.
fallacies.body: A critic's affiliation or loyalty does not determine whether the criticism is true. The accusation makes disagreement socially costly and shifts attention from the evidence.

examples.text: The employee's safety report is disloyal to the company, so its findings should be ignored.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The critic is branded a traitor or disloyal, and that label is used to avoid the claim.
doesNotCountWhen: A proven breach of duty may be relevant to conduct, but it does not refute the factual content of a criticism.

fallacies.name: Treating nonsignificance as proof of no effect
fallacies.summary: Treating a statistically non-significant result as proof that an effect is exactly zero.
fallacies.body: A non-significant result means the study did not distinguish the estimate from zero at a chosen threshold; it may reflect low power or wide uncertainty. Evidence of absence needs sufficiently precise estimates or an equivalence test.

examples.text: A small trial finds no significant benefit, so the treatment has no effect.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Failure to reject a null hypothesis is interpreted as confirmation of no effect without considering uncertainty or power.
doesNotCountWhen: A well-powered equivalence study with a narrow interval can support the conclusion that any effect is practically negligible.

fallacies.name: Treating zero observed events as zero risk
fallacies.summary: Inferring that a risk is zero because no events occurred in a limited sample or observation period.
fallacies.body: Zero observed cases can still be compatible with a nonzero underlying rate, especially when the sample is small. The conclusion should account for sample size and uncertainty.

examples.text: No failures occurred in 20 tests, so the machine has a zero failure rate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The absence of observed events is converted into a claim of impossible risk.
doesNotCountWhen: A zero-risk claim requires a strong mechanistic or mathematical basis, not merely a finite run with no events.

fallacies.name: Trivial objections
fallacies.summary: Using a minor or irrelevant criticism to suggest that a central claim has been refuted.
fallacies.body: A small flaw may deserve correction but does not necessarily affect the main conclusion. The response exaggerates its importance or uses it to avoid stronger evidence.

examples.text: A report misspells one street name, so its traffic counts must be false.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A minor defect is made to carry more evidential weight than it has for the core claim.
doesNotCountWhen: A seemingly small error is substantial when it undermines the measurement or reasoning central to the conclusion.

fallacies.name: Tu quoque
fallacies.summary: Rejecting criticism by accusing the critic of the same behavior instead of addressing whether the criticism is true.
fallacies.body: Hypocrisy may reduce credibility or reveal inconsistent standards, but it does not answer the claim. The critic's conduct and the truth of the criticism are separate questions.

examples.text: You tell us to reduce waste, but you drive a large car, so reducing waste is pointless.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reply points to the critic's inconsistency as a refutation of the criticism itself.
doesNotCountWhen: A critic's inconsistency can be relevant to applying standards fairly, while leaving the underlying claim to be evaluated.

fallacies.name: Two wrongs make a right
fallacies.summary: Claiming that one wrong action is justified because someone else acted wrongly first.
fallacies.body: A prior wrong may explain retaliation or affect responsibility, but it does not automatically make the response permissible. The justification needs its own moral or legal basis, such as proportionate defense.

examples.text: They damaged our fence, so we are entitled to damage theirs.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Another person's misconduct is offered as sufficient justification for a separate wrong.
doesNotCountWhen: A proportionate response to prevent harm may be justified by necessity, not by the slogan that two wrongs cancel.

fallacies.name: Type–token fallacy
fallacies.summary: Confusing an abstract kind of thing with a particular instance of that kind.
fallacies.body: A type is a category or design; a token is one concrete occurrence. Claims about the type do not always apply to a specific token, and one token's properties do not automatically characterize every instance.

examples.text: The word “tree” has four letters, so every tree has four letters.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A property of a word/type is transferred to its instances or vice versa without a valid link.
doesNotCountWhen: A type-level claim applies to tokens when the property is genuinely shared by all instances.

fallacies.name: Undistributed middle
fallacies.summary: In a categorical syllogism, using a middle category that is not shown to overlap the subject and predicate classes.
fallacies.body: The premises may say that both groups share a broad category, but not that they share members with each other. The middle term must connect the classes, not merely be present in both statements.

examples.text: All cats are mammals; all dogs are mammals; therefore all dogs are cats.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The middle term is undistributed in both premises, so no overlap between the other terms is established.
doesNotCountWhen: The conclusion follows when a premise identifies the relevant members or the middle term is distributed validly.

fallacies.name: Unfalsifiable defense
fallacies.summary: Protecting a claim by adding explanations that make every possible observation compatible with it.
fallacies.body: A claim that cannot lose support under any outcome cannot be tested against alternatives. The problem is not that every useful claim must be easily falsifiable, but that this defense treats all counterevidence as confirmation.

examples.text: The prediction failed because the effect is invisible; if it had succeeded, that would prove the effect was visible.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: No conceivable result is allowed to count against the claim, due to a protective reinterpretation.
doesNotCountWhen: A theory may have indirect tests, but it needs some observable outcomes that would count against it.

fallacies.name: Unreasonable inclusion
fallacies.summary: Including cases in a category despite failing its relevant criteria, in order to inflate or distort the conclusion.
fallacies.body: Definitions should be applied consistently. Counting borderline or ineligible cases without justification can make a group seem larger, more successful, or more representative than it is.

examples.text: A program counts people who only viewed its website as “graduates” to report a high completion rate.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The category's membership is expanded beyond its stated or defensible criteria to support a claim.
doesNotCountWhen: Broad inclusion is reasonable when the criteria are explicit, relevant, and applied consistently.

fallacies.name: Unrepresentative generalization
fallacies.summary: Generalizing from cases that do not reflect the population or context the claim concerns.
fallacies.body: Even many observations can mislead if they come from a skewed source. The sample must resemble the target population on features that affect the outcome.

examples.text: A survey at a luxury resort is used to describe typical household spending nationwide.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The observed cases differ systematically from the population the conclusion describes.
doesNotCountWhen: A limited conclusion about the sampled setting is valid; population claims need representative evidence or adjustment.

fallacies.name: Unsupported conspiracy explanation
fallacies.summary: Explaining an event as a coordinated secret plot without sufficient evidence for the alleged coordination.
fallacies.body: Conspiracies can occur, but a complex plot requires evidence of actors, communication, and mechanisms. Treating every gap or contradiction as proof of concealment makes the theory self-protecting.

examples.text: Several agencies issue similar guidance, so they must secretly coordinate to deceive the public, with no evidence of contact.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The account asserts hidden coordination and explains missing evidence as further proof, without independent support.
doesNotCountWhen: A conspiracy claim is credible when documentary, testimonial, or circumstantial evidence supports specific coordination and alternatives are considered.

fallacies.name: Unsupported counterfactual
fallacies.summary: Claiming what would have happened under an alternative scenario without evidence for the imagined outcome.
fallacies.body: Counterfactuals can be useful, but only when grounded in causal models or comparable cases. The unobserved alternative cannot simply be asserted to support a preferred story.

examples.text: If the city had not built the road, every local business would have closed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A claim about an unobserved alternative outcome is stated as fact without a credible causal basis.
doesNotCountWhen: A counterfactual is reasoned when supported by a model, natural experiment, or relevant comparison, with uncertainty noted.

fallacies.name: Unwarranted contrast
fallacies.summary: Implying a difference or opposition between two things when the evidence does not establish one.
fallacies.body: Phrases like “even,” “still,” or “unlike” can suggest that a contrast is meaningful. The argument uses that implication to guide judgment without showing the relevant comparison.

examples.text: The new team met its target, unlike the previous team, though the targets and conditions differed.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A contrast is used to imply a meaningful difference without comparable evidence.
doesNotCountWhen: A contrast is fair when the compared cases and metric are sufficiently aligned.

fallacies.name: Use–mention error
fallacies.summary: Confusing a word or phrase with the thing the word refers to.
fallacies.body: Mentioning a word is different from using it to talk about its referent. The error shifts between those levels, often producing a category mistake about language itself.

examples.text: “Fire” has four letters, so the fire is small.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: A property of the expression is attributed to its referent, or vice versa.
doesNotCountWhen: Quoting or discussing a word as a word is clear when quotation or other marking preserves the distinction.

fallacies.name: We-have-to-do-something fallacy
fallacies.summary: Treating the need to act as proof that a particular proposed action is effective or appropriate.
fallacies.body: A problem may demand attention, but urgency does not identify the right intervention. The proposal still needs a causal rationale and comparison with alternatives, including unintended consequences.

examples.text: The river is polluted, so impose this untested ban immediately because action is better than none.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The general need for action is used to bypass evidence about the specific action proposed.
doesNotCountWhen: Acting under uncertainty can be reasonable when delay is costly and the measure is supported by the best available assessment.

fallacies.name: Weak man
fallacies.summary: Responding to a vaguely or minimally stated opponent position without engaging its strongest clear version.
fallacies.body: A weak-man response may omit the opponent's central evidence or qualifications, making rebuttal easier. Unlike a straw man, the replacement can be more a thin caricature or underdeveloped paraphrase than an explicit distortion.

examples.text: A detailed argument for changing one zoning rule is answered with “you just dislike development.”

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The reply addresses a shallow or incomplete version while leaving the actual reasoning untouched.
doesNotCountWhen: A concise summary is adequate when it captures the strongest relevant point and the response engages it.

fallacies.name: Whataboutism
fallacies.summary: Deflecting criticism by pointing to another person's or group's alleged wrongdoing instead of addressing the criticism.
fallacies.body: The comparison may identify a real inconsistency, but it does not answer whether the original conduct occurred or was justified. The two issues should be evaluated separately.

examples.text: Asked about its own emissions, a company replies that a competitor pollutes more.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The response changes the subject to another case and treats that comparison as a defense.
doesNotCountWhen: Comparisons are relevant to consistency or relative priority, but do not erase the original claim.

fallacies.name: Wishful thinking
fallacies.summary: Treating a desired outcome as likely or true because one wants it to happen.
fallacies.body: Hope can motivate effort, but it does not change evidence or probability. The reasoning confuses preference with a forecast or fact.

examples.text: We need the merger to succeed, so it will certainly increase revenue.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: Desirability is used as support for a factual prediction or belief.
doesNotCountWhen: Optimism is reasonable when based on evidence and expressed at a confidence level the evidence supports.

fallacies.name: Worst-negates-the-bad fallacy
aliases: be grateful for what you have
fallacies.summary: Claiming an option is good because it avoids the worst possible outcome, without comparing it with better feasible options.
fallacies.body: Avoiding catastrophe matters, but that alone does not show a proposal is wise or fair. The argument treats “not the worst” as “good enough” without considering opportunity costs.

examples.text: This plan prevents total shutdown, so it is the best plan, though a less costly option would also prevent it.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The proposal is endorsed only because it avoids a worst case, with feasible alternatives left unexamined.
doesNotCountWhen: Choosing a merely adequate option is sound when constraints make better alternatives unavailable or disproportionate.

fallacies.name: Zero-tolerance fallacy
fallacies.summary: Assuming a rule must allow no exceptions or discretion to be effective or fair.
fallacies.body: Strict rules can deter misconduct, but zero tolerance may punish harmless or accidental cases disproportionately. Effectiveness and fairness depend on the rule's design, context, and consequences.

examples.text: A school suspends every student who brings a tool, including one who unknowingly has a permitted craft item, because any exception would make the rule useless.

fallacies.detectionCriteria: The argument treats discretion or proportional exceptions as equivalent to abandoning the rule.
doesNotCountWhen: A strict threshold is justified when its purpose, notice, and consequences support uniform application without disproportionate harm.
